Tier structure of strongly endotactic reaction networks

This document was conceived and prepared while all the authors were working at the Department of Mathematics of the University of Wisconsin-Madison.
David F. Anderson Note: Department of Mathematics, University of Wisconsin-Madison, anderson@math.wisc.edu. Grant support from NSF-DMS-1318832 and Army Research Office W911NF-14-1-0401.    Daniele Cappelletti Note: Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering, ETH Zürich, daniele.cappelletti@bsse.ethz.ch.    Jinsu Kim Note: Department of Mathematics, University of California, Irvine, jinsu.kim@uci.edu.    Tung Nguyen Note: Department of Mathematics, University of Wisconsin-Madison, nguyen34@wisc.edu.
Abstract

Reaction networks are mainly used to model the time-evolution of molecules of interacting chemical species. Stochastic models are typically used when the counts of the molecules are low, whereas deterministic models are often used when the counts are in high abundance. The mathematical study of reaction networks has increased dramatically over the last two decades as these models are now routinely used to investigate cellular behavior. In 2011, the notion of “tiers” was introduced to study the long time behavior of deterministically modeled reaction networks that are weakly reversible and have a single linkage class. This “tier” based argument was analytical in nature. Later, in 2014, the notion of a strongly endotactic network was introduced in order to generalize the previous results from weakly reversible networks with a single linkage class to this wider family of networks. The point of view of this later work was more geometric and algebraic in nature. The notion of strongly endotactic networks was later used in 2018 to prove a large deviation principle for a class of stochastically modeled reaction networks.

In the current paper we provide an analytical characterization of strongly endotactic networks in terms of tier structures. By doing so, we not only shed light on the connection between the two points of view, but also make available a new proof technique for the study of strongly endotactic networks. We show the power of this new technique in two distinct ways. First, we demonstrate how the main previous results related to strongly endotactic networks, both for the deterministic and stochastic modeling choices, can be quickly obtained from our characterization. Second, we demonstrate how new results can be obtained by proving that a sub-class of strongly endotactic networks, when modeled stochastically, is positive recurrent. Finally, and similarly to recent independent work by Agazzi and Mattingly, we provide an example which closes a conjecture in the negative by showing that stochastically modeled strongly endotactic networks can be transient (and even explosive).

1 Introduction

Reaction networks are now commonly used to model the dynamical behavior of cellular processes, including gene regulatory systems, signaling systems, metabolic systems, viral infections, etc. If the counts of the constituent “species” of the system of interest are low, then the dynamics of the counts are typically modeled via a continuous-time Markov chain with state space ℤ≥0d\mathbb{Z}^{d}_{\geq 0}, where dd is the number of species in the system. On the other hand, if the counts are high, then an autonomous system of (typically non-linear) ordinary differential equations in ℝ≥0d\mathbb{R}^{d}_{\geq 0} is used to model the dynamics of the relevant chemical concentrations. See [11, 30, 29] for the precise connection between these two modeling choices.

The mathematical foundation of deterministically modeled reaction networks can largely be traced back to the series of papers [20, 25, 26], where Feinberg, Horn, and Jackson introduced the notion of network deficiency and proved that if the reaction network (i) is weakly reversibility and (ii) has a deficiency of zero, then the resulting deterministically modeled system endowed with mass-action kinetics is “complex-balanced,” which means that (i) every linear invariant manifold in ℝ>0d\mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0} admits precisely one equilibrium point, and (ii) each of these equilibria satisfies a particular network balance and it is a so-called complex-balanced equilibrium. Importantly, they showed that this result holds regardless of the choice of rate parameters for the model. Feinberg, Horn, and Jackson were interested in chemical systems at an industrial scale. At smaller scales, discrete stochastic models have been utilized and studied. In particular, the works of Gardiner [21], Van Kampen [35], Kurtz [30, 29, 28], and Gillespie [22, 23] were all instrumental in increasing our understanding of these models.

Much of the work cited in the previous paragraph took place in the 1960s and 1970s. While there was mathematical work related to reaction networks during the 1980s and 1990s, it was the advent of new technologies in the biological setting, such as fluorescent proteins, that made the study of mathematical models of reaction networks quite popular over the last two decades.

Reaction networks can naturally be associated with a finite graph, constituted by the set of all chemical reactions that can take place. For a few examples of such graphs, see Examples 3.1, 3.2, and 3.3. Much of the theory on reaction networks deals with connections between such finite graphs, which are relatively easy to study, and the qualitative properties of the associated dynamical system. We note also that it is most useful to provide results that hold for any choice of model parameters, as these parameters are often unknown with any certainty in the biological setting. Specifically, the mathematical results about reaction networks are often of the following form:

Consider a reaction network whose associated graph has properties A, B, and C. Then, for any choice of parameters for the model, the relevant dynamical system will have property D.

For example, in the works of Horn, Jackson, and Feinberg cited above, weak reversibility and a deficiency of zero are both structural properties of the graph, and they imply qualitative dynamical properties of the models such as non-chaotic behavior of the trajectories and the absence of limit cycles, regardless of the choice of model parameters.

For our purposes, the most relevant previous works in the field are [4, 5] by Anderson, [24] by Gopalkrishnan, Miller, and Shiu, and [1, 2] by Agazzi, Dembo, and Eckmann. In [4, 5], Anderson developed the concept of “tiers” of complexes, and used them to study deterministically modeled reaction networks. Loosely speaking, tiers constitute a partition of the system complexes (see section 2 for relevant definitions) into sets related to reactions whose propensities have the same relative strength along a particular sequence of points in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. The works [4, 5] used tiers to prove that trajectories for reactions networks that were (i) weakly reversible and (ii) had a single linkage class, were necessarily persistent (meaning that they cannot get arbitrarily close to the boundary of the state space, see Definition 5.1) and bounded, regardless of the choice of rate parameters. These works closed the well-known Global Attractor Conjecture in the single linkage class case [16]. Later, in [24], Gopalkrishnan, Miller, and Shiu (i) introduced the notion of strongly endotactic networks (which are a subclass of endotactic networks, introduced in [17]), (ii) showed that weakly reversible networks that have a single linkage class are strongly endotactic, and (iii) showed that deterministically modeled strongly endotactic networks are permanent (which is a stronger condition than persistence and boundedness of trajectories, see Definition 5.2). The main results of [24] are stated here as Theorems 5.4 and 5.5. Finally, the class of strongly endotactic networks have been fruitfully recently considered in [1, 2], where a large deviation principle for stochastically modeled reaction networks that are strongly endotactic and that are also “asiphonic” is provided.

The tier argument developed in [5, 4] was analytical in nature, whereas the methods developed in [24] and later utilized in [1, 2], while quite similar to those developed in [5, 4], were more algebraic and geometric in nature. In the present work, we will make the connections between the two works more precise. Specifically, we will characterize strongly endotactic networks in regards to their tier structures.

Elucidating the connection between strongly endotactic networks and tiers is the first major contribution of this work, and provides a new proof technique for the study of strongly endotactic networks. We will demonstrate the power of this new technique in two distinct ways.

  1. 1.

    We show how the proofs of the major results related to strongly endotactic networks in both the deterministic and stochastic settings can be dramatically streamlined. First, we will show how the main results of [24] related to deterministic models of reaction networks that are strongly endotactic follow in a straightforward manner by the tier characterization. Second, we will show how the main analytical results of [1, 2] can be quickly recovered using our characterization.

  2. 2.

    We show that members of a particular subclass of strongly endotactic networks are positive recurrent when modeled stochastically, regardless of the choice of rate parameters.

We make one further contribution in this paper. It has been proven in a number of instances that the behaviors of the associated deterministic and stochastic models for reaction networks are similar in a broad sense. For example, there is theory connecting the dynamics of the two models on compact time intervals [29, 30, 7], on pathwise approximations [14, 15], and on similarities between their long time stationary behavior [9, 6, 13, 12]. Hence, since it is proven in [24] that deterministically modeled strongly endotactic networks have very well behaved trajectories in the sense made precise by Theorems 5.4 and 5.5, it was natural to conjecture that all strongly endotactic networks are necessarily positive recurrent when stochastically modeled. We show this conjecture to be false by providing strongly endotactic networks that are transient and even explosive, regardless of the choice of parameters for the model (see Examples 3.1 and 3.2). (We note that the conjecture has independently been shown to be false in the recently submitted paper [3] by Mattingly and Agazzi, where other examples are provided.)

The outline of the remainder of the paper is as follows. In section 2, we provide useful notation, and the relevant mathematical models. In section 3, we provide the definition of a strongly endotactic network. We also provide the examples alluded to in the previous paragraph demonstrating that not all strongly endotactic networks are recurrent, when modeled stochastically. In section 4, we provide the relevant definitions pertaining to tiers. In particular, in subsection 4.2 we provide our main analytical result, Theorem 4.2, that characterizes strongly endotactic networks by their tier structures. In section 5, we use our results from section 4 to prove that deterministically modeled strongly endotactic networks are both persistent and permanent. Therefore, the results of section 5 recover the main findings in [24]. In section 6, we utilize our results from section 4 to recover a sufficient condition used in [1, 2] to prove a large deviation principle. Finally, in section 7, we use the results of section 4 to provide a new subclass of reaction networks for which positive recurrence is guaranteed, regardless of the choice of rate parameters.

2 Background

2.1 Notation

Throughout the paper, we will denote by ℝ\mathbb{R}, ℝ≥0\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}, and ℝ>0\mathbb{R}_{>0} the real, the non-negative real, and the positive real numbers, respectively. Similarly, we will denote by ℤ\mathbb{Z}, ℤ≥0\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, and ℤ>0\mathbb{Z}_{>0} the integer, the non-negative integer, and the positive integer numbers, respectively. Given a vector v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, we say that the vector is positive or non-negative if vv is in ℝ>0d\mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0} or ℝ≥0d\mathbb{R}^{d}_{\geq 0}, respectively.

Given two vectors v,w∈ℝdv,w\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, we will denote by ⟨v,w⟩\langle v,w\rangle their scalar product. Furthermore, we will write v≥wv\geq w if the inequality holds component-wise. Moreover, we will use the following shorthand notation:

vw=∏i=1dviwi,v!=∏i=1dvi!,v^{w}=\prod_{i=1}^{d}v_{i}^{w_{i}},\quad v!=\prod_{i=1}^{d}v_{i}!,

where we use the usual convention 00=10^{0}=1. Finally, we will denote by ln⁡(v)\ln(v) the vector of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} whose iith entry is ln⁡(vi)\ln(v_{i}) and we will denote by ⌊v⌋\lfloor v\rfloor the vector whose iith entry is ⌊vi⌋\lfloor v_{i}\rfloor.

Given a vector v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, we denote

‖v‖∞=max⁡{|vi|: 1≤i≤d}and‖v‖1=∑i=1d|vi|.\|v\|_{\infty}=\max\{|v_{i}|\,:\,1\leq i\leq d\}\quad\text{and}\quad\|v\|_{1}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}|v_{i}|.

2.2 Reaction networks

A reaction network is a triple 𝒢=(𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) where 𝒮\mathcal{S}, 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and ℛ\mathcal{R} are defined as follows. 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a finite set of species, that is a set of dd distinct symbols. 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a finite set of complexes. We assume each complex is a linear combinations of species on ℤ≥0\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. Complexes will be regarded as vectors in ℤ≥0d\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{d} in the paper, given that an ordering for the species is chosen. Finally, ℛ\mathcal{R} is a finite set of reactions, that is a finite subset of 𝒞×𝒞\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{C} with the property that for any y∈𝒞y\in\mathcal{C} we have (y,y)∉ℛ(y,y)\notin\mathcal{R}. Usually, a reaction (y,y′)(y,y^{\prime}) is denoted by y→y′y\to y^{\prime}, and we adopt this notation in the paper.

We say that yy is a source complex if there is a reaction of the form y→y′y\to y^{\prime}, and we say that yy is a product complex if there is a reaction of the form y′→yy^{\prime}\to y. Moreover, given a reaction y→y′y\to y^{\prime} we say that yy is the source and y′y^{\prime} is the product of y→y′y\to y^{\prime}.

It is often convenient to denote the species as {S1,…,Sd}\{S_{1},\dots,S_{d}\}, as this allows us to refer to species via their index. In particular, we will write both Si∈𝒮S_{i}\in\mathcal{S} and i∈𝒮i\in\mathcal{S}. However, in practical examples the set of species is often given as some subset of {A,B,C,…}\{A,B,C,\dots\}.

Given a reaction network 𝒢\mathcal{G}, a directed graph with nodes 𝒞\mathcal{C} and edges ℛ\mathcal{R} can be constructed. This directed graph is called reaction graph. See Examples 3.1, 3.2, and 3.3 for examples of such graphs. In this paper we assume that all complexes appear in at least one reaction and all species appear in at least one complex. Under this assumption, the reaction graph uniquely determines a reaction network. In fact, reaction networks are usually described by means of their reaction graph, and the same will be done in the present paper.

The stoichiometric subspace is defined as

S=spanℝ⁡{y′−y:y→y′∈ℛ},S=\spann_{\mathbb{R}}\{y^{\prime}-y\,:\,y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}\},

and for any x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} the set x+S={x+s, with ​s∈S}x+S=\{x+s,\text{ with }s\in S\} is termed the stoichiometric compatibility class determined by xx. Similarly, the sets (x+S)∩ℝ≥0d(x+S)\cap\mathbb{R}^{d}_{\geq 0} are the nonnegative stoichiometric compatibility classes.

2.3 Deterministic model

Deterministic models are typically used when the counts of the relevant molecules (the species) are large and their concentrations change nearly continuously in time accordingly to the propensities of the different chemical transformations.

Formally, given a reaction network 𝒢\mathcal{G}, a (deterministic) kinetics Λ\Lambda for 𝒢\mathcal{G} is a map assigning a function λy→y′:ℝ≥0d→ℝ≥0\lambda_{y\to y^{\prime}}:\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} to each reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}. The functions λy→y′\lambda_{y\to y^{\prime}} are called (deterministic) rate functions. We call a pair (𝒢,Λ)(\mathcal{G},\Lambda), where 𝒢\mathcal{G} is a reaction network and Λ\Lambda is a deterministic kinetics, a deterministic reaction system. In this setting, the concentration of the different chemical species is of interest, which should be understood as the average number of molecules of the different species per unit of volume. If molecules are approximated with dimensionless points in space, concentrations are non-negative real numbers ranging from 0 to ∞\infty. Given an initial condition z⁡(0)∈ℝ≥0dz(0)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}_{\geq 0}, the change in chemical species concentration is then modeled as the solution to the integral equation

z⁡(t)=z⁡(0)+∑y→y′∈ℛ(y′−y)​∫0tλy→y′​(z⁡(s))​𝑑s,z(t)=z(0)+\sum_{y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}(y^{\prime}-y)\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{y\to y^{\prime}}(z(s))\,ds, (2.1)

if the solution exists and is unique. Note that at any time point tt, z⁡(t)−z⁡(0)∈Sz(t)-z(0)\in S. That is, z⁡(t)z(t) is confined within the same stoichiometric compatibility class as z⁡(0)z(0).

A popular choice of kinetics is given by (deterministic) mass action kinetics, where for any reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}, the associated rate function is given by

λy→y′D​(x)=κy→y′​xy,\lambda^{D}_{y\to y^{\prime}}(x)=\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}x^{y},

for some positive constant κy→y′\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}, termed a reaction constant. Note that under the assumption of mass action kinetics, the solution to (2.1) exists and is unique for any initial condition, since the rates λy→y′\lambda_{y\to y^{\prime}} are polynomials and therefore locally Lipschitz. In contrast, global existence is not guaranteed, and in case of a blow-up at a finite time t⋆t^{\star} we consider the solution to (2.1) only in the interval [0,t⋆)[0,t^{\star}).

Mass action kinetics corresponds to the hypothesis that the molecules of the chemical species involved in the transformations are well-stirred. In the present paper, we will focus on this choice of kinetics, which is typically studied in reaction network theory [19] and in biochemistry [18, 27]. More general kinetics (such as Michaelis-Menten kinetics) can be derived as limits of mass action kinetics when different chemical reactions operate over time scales of different orders of magnitude [18, 27].

2.4 Stochastic model

Stochastic models are typically used when we are interested in the counts of the different chemical species. This situation typically arises when the abundances are low, as is often the case in the biological setting.

The formal definition of stochastic reaction systems follows the definition of deterministic reaction systems closely: given a reaction network 𝒢\mathcal{G}, a (stochastic) kinetics Λ\Lambda for 𝒢\mathcal{G} is a map assigning a function λy→y′:ℤ≥0d→ℝ≥0\lambda_{y\to y^{\prime}}:\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} to each reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}. The functions λy→y′\lambda_{y\to y^{\prime}} are called (stochastic) rate functions. A stochastic reaction system is a pair (𝒢,Λ)(\mathcal{G},\Lambda), where 𝒢\mathcal{G} is a reaction network and Λ\Lambda is a stochastic kinetics. The change in chemical species counts is modeled by means of a continuous-time Markov chain with state space ℤ≥0d\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{d}, whose transition rates are given by

q⁡(x,x+ξ)=∑y→y′∈ℛy′−y=ξλy→y′​(x).q(x,x+\xi)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}\\ y^{\prime}-y=\xi\end{subarray}}\lambda_{y\to y^{\prime}}(x).

In case of an explosion occurring at a finite-time T∞T_{\infty}, we consider the X⁡(t)=ΔX(t)=\Delta for any t≥T∞t\geq T_{\infty}, where Δ\Delta is a cemetery state not contained in ℤ≥0d\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{d}. Another representation of the Markov chain XX, due to Kurtz [31], is given as follows:

X⁡(t)=X⁡(0)+∑y→y′∈ℛ(y′−y)​Yy→y′​(∫0tλy→y′​(X⁡(s))​𝑑s)\displaystyle X(t)=X(0)+\sum_{y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}(y^{\prime}-y)Y_{y\to y^{\prime}}\left(\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{y\to y^{\prime}}(X(s))\,ds\right) (2.2)

where Yy→y′Y_{y\to y^{\prime}} are independent, unit-rate Poisson processes. Letting TnT_{n} denote the time of the nnth transition of the model, the above representation is valid up until T∞=limn→∞TnT_{\infty}=\lim_{n\to\infty}T_{n}. Here, the counting process

Ry→y′​(t)=Yy→y′​(∫0tλy→y′​(X⁡(s))​𝑑s)R_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t)=Y_{y\to y^{\prime}}\left(\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{y\to y^{\prime}}(X(s))\,ds\right)

keeps track of how many times the reaction y→y′y\to y^{\prime} has occurred by time tt.

From (2.2) we have that X⁡(t)−X⁡(0)∈SX(t)-X(0)\in S for any time point tt. Hence, and just as for the deterministic model, the stochastic process XX is confined within the stoichiometric compatibility class determined by X⁡(0)X(0).

A popular choice of stochastic kinetics is given by (stochastic) mass action kinetics, where for any reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}

λy→y′S(x)=κy→y′𝟙{x≥y}x!(x−y)!,\displaystyle\lambda^{S}_{y\to y^{\prime}}(x)=\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}\mathbbm{1}_{\{x\geq y\}}\frac{x!}{(x-y)!}, (2.3)

for some positive constant κy→y′\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}, called a reaction constant. Similarly with deterministic reaction networks, mass action kinetics corresponds to the hypothesis that the molecules are well-stirred in space. The analysis of the present paper focus on this choice of kinetics.

3 Strongly endotactic networks

We give here the definition of strongly endotactic networks, that was first introduced in [24].

Definition 3.1.

Consider a reaction network 𝒢\mathcal{G}, and a vector w∈ℝdw\in\mathbb{R}^{d} that is not orthogonal to the stoichiometric subspace SS. We say that a complex y∈𝒞y\in\mathcal{C} is w−w-maximal if yy is a source complex and for any other source complex y′y^{\prime} we have ⟨w,y′−y⟩≤0\langle w,y^{\prime}-y\rangle\leq 0.

Definition 3.2.

A reaction network 𝒢\mathcal{G} is strongly endotactic if for all vectors w∈ℝdw\in\mathbb{R}^{d} that are not orthogonal to the stoichiometric subspace SS the following holds:

  1. 1.

    if yy is a w−w-maximal complex, then for all reactions of the form y→y′y\to y^{\prime} we have ⟨w,y′−y⟩≤0\langle w,y^{\prime}-y\rangle\leq 0;

  2. 2.

    there exists a w−w-maximal complex yy and a reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} with ⟨w,y′−y⟩<0\langle w,y^{\prime}-y\rangle<0.

Strongly endotactic networks are a generalization of weakly reversible single linkage class networks studied in [5]: the following proposition, which is corollary 3.20 in [24], makes the statement precise.

Proposition 3.1.

Assume 𝒢\mathcal{G} is a reaction network such that for any two complexes y,y′y,y^{\prime} there exists a sequence of ℓ\ell complexes, y=y1,y2,…,yℓ=y′y=y_{1},y_{2},\dots,y_{\ell}=y^{\prime}, such that yj→yj+1∈ℛy_{j}\to y_{j+1}\in\mathcal{R} for all 1≤j≤ℓ−11\leq j\leq\ell-1 (this condition is equivalent to saying that 𝒢\mathcal{G} is weakly reversible and consists of a single linkage class). Then, 𝒢\mathcal{G} is strongly endotactic.

Strongly endotactic network are not necessarily weakly reversible single linkage class networks, examples are provided in Examples 3.1 and 3.2. As discussed in the Introduction, due to the stable behavior of the deterministic mass action systems associated with strongly endotactic networks (see Theorems 5.4 and 5.5), it was conjectured that stochastic mass action systems associated to strongly endotactic networks would be positive recurrent for any choice of rate constants. This is not the case: in Example 3.1 a strongly endotactic network is considered that results in a transient system if endowed with stochastic mass action kinetics, for any choice of rate constants. Furthermore, in Example 3.2 we show that a similar model is explosive for any choice of rate constants.

Example 3.1.

Consider the reaction network

0→2​A+B→4​A+4​B→A.0\to 2A+B\to 4A+4B\to A.

The reaction network is strongly endotactic: to check that this statement is true, it is convenient to draw the complexes considered as vectors on a Cartesian plane, and depict the reactions as arrows among them. This is done in Figure 1(a). Now consider the shaded regions of Figure 1(b): it can be checked that

  • •

    If w∈R1w\in R_{1}, then the w−w-maximal complex is 4​A+4​B4A+4B. The only reaction with source complex 4​A+4​B4A+4B is 4​A+4​B→A4A+4B\to A, and we have ⟨w,(−3,−4)⟩<0\langle w,(-3,-4)\rangle<0.

  • •

    If w∈R2w\in R_{2}, then the w−w-maximal complex is 00. The only reaction with source complex 00 is 0→2​A+B0\to 2A+B, and we have ⟨w,(2,1)⟩<0\langle w,(2,1)\rangle<0.

  • •

    If w∈R3w\in R_{3}, then the w−w-maximal complex is 2​A+B2A+B. The only reaction with source complex 2​A+B2A+B is 2​A+B→4​A+4​B2A+B\to 4A+4B, and we have ⟨w,(2,3)⟩<0\langle w,(2,3)\rangle<0.

  • •

    If ww is a positive multiple of (−1,1)(-1,1), then the w−w-maximal complexes are 00 and 4​A+4​B4A+4B, which are source complexes of 0→2​A+B0\to 2A+B and 4​A+4​B→A4A+4B\to A. In this case, we have ⟨w,(2,1)⟩<0\langle w,(2,1)\rangle<0 and ⟨w,(−3,−4)⟩<0\langle w,(-3,-4)\rangle<0.

  • •

    If ww is a positive multiple of (1,−2)(1,-2), then the w−w-maximal complexes are 00 and 2​A+B2A+B, which are source complexes of 0→2​A+B0\to 2A+B and 2​A+B→4​A+4​B2A+B\to 4A+4B. In this case, we have ⟨w,(2,1)⟩=0\langle w,(2,1)\rangle=0 and ⟨w,(2,3)⟩<0\langle w,(2,3)\rangle<0.

  • •

    If ww is a positive multiple of (1,−2/3)(1,-2/3), then the w−w-maximal complexes are 2​A+B2A+B and 4​A+4​B4A+4B, which are source complexes of 2​A+B→4​A+4​B2A+B\to 4A+4B and 4​A+4​B→A4A+4B\to A. In this case, we have ⟨w,(2,3)⟩=0\langle w,(2,3)\rangle=0 and ⟨w,(−3,−4)⟩<0\langle w,(-3,-4)\rangle<0.

Hence, the network is strongly endotactic. A general strategy to recognize strongly endotactic network, called the sweep test, and which we essentially carried out here in detail, is discussed in [24].

Nevertheless, any stochastic mass action system associated with the network is transient. Indeed, from any state x=(xA,xB)∈ℤdx=(x_{A},x_{B})\in\mathbb{Z}^{d} there is a positive probability that the reaction 0→2​A+B0\to 2A+B occurs jj consecutive times, with xA+2​j≥xB+jx_{A}+2j\geq x_{B}+j and xB+jx_{B}+j being divisible by 4. There is then a positive probability that the reaction 4​A+4​B→04A+4B\to 0 takes place until no molecule of BB is left, and a state of the form x′=(xA′,0)x^{\prime}=(x^{\prime}_{A},0) is reached. Then, due to continuity of probability measures, the probability, p⁡(xA′),p(x_{A}^{\prime}), that from the state x′x^{\prime} the infinite repetition of the sequence of reactions 0→2​A+B0\to 2A+B, 2​A+B→4​A+4​B2A+B\to 4A+4B and 4​A+4​B→A4A+4B\to A take place is

p⁡(xA′)=∏n=xA′+1∞1\displaystyle p(x^{\prime}_{A})=\prod_{n=x^{\prime}_{A}+1}^{\infty}1 ⋅κ2​A+B→4​A+4​B​(n+1)​nκ2​A+B→4​A+4​B​(n+1)​n+κ0→2​A+B\displaystyle\cdot\frac{\kappa_{2A+B\to 4A+4B}(n+1)n}{\kappa_{2A+B\to 4A+4B}(n+1)n+\kappa_{0\to 2A+B}}
⋅κ4​A+4​B→A​(n+3)​(n+2)​(n+1)​n⋅4!κ4​A+4​B→A​(n+3)​(n+2)​(n+1)​n⋅4!+κ2​A+B→4​A+4​B​(n+3)​(n+2)⋅4+κ0→2​A+B.\displaystyle\cdot\frac{\kappa_{4A+4B\to A}(n+3)(n+2)(n+1)n\cdot 4!}{\kappa_{4A+4B\to A}(n+3)(n+2)(n+1)n\cdot 4!+\kappa_{2A+B\to 4A+4B}(n+3)(n+2)\cdot 4+\kappa_{0\to 2A+B}}.

An infinite product of the form ∏nan​bn\prod_{n}a_{n}b_{n}, where an,bn∈(0,1)a_{n},b_{n}\in(0,1), will converge to a nonzero value if and only if the infinite sum ∑n[(1−an)+(1−bn)]\sum_{n}\left[(1-a_{n})+(1-b_{n})\right] converges; see [34, Theorem 15.4]. The sum

∑n=xA′+1∞\displaystyle\sum_{n=x^{\prime}_{A}+1}^{\infty} (κ0→2​A+Bκ2​A+B→4​A+4​B​(n+1)​n+κ0→2​A+B+CLOSE\displaystyle\Bigg(\frac{\kappa_{0\to 2A+B}}{\kappa_{2A+B\to 4A+4B}(n+1)n+\kappa_{0\to 2A+B}}+
OPEN+κ2​A+B→4​A+4​B​(n+3)​(n+2)⋅4+κ0→2​A+Bκ4​A+4​B→A​(n+3)​(n+2)​(n+1)​n⋅4!+κ2​A+B→4​A+4​B​(n+3)​(n+2)⋅4+κ0→2​A+B)<∞,\displaystyle+\frac{\kappa_{2A+B\to 4A+4B}(n+3)(n+2)\cdot 4+\kappa_{0\to 2A+B}}{\kappa_{4A+4B\to A}(n+3)(n+2)(n+1)n\cdot 4!+\kappa_{2A+B\to 4A+4B}(n+3)(n+2)\cdot 4+\kappa_{0\to 2A+B}}\Bigg)<\infty,

has terms of order n−2n^{-2}, and so converges. Thus, we may conclude that p⁡(xA′)>0p(x^{\prime}_{A})>0. Hence, it follows that there is a positive probability of leaving the state xx forever through the repetition of the sequence of reactions 0→2​A+B0\to 2A+B, 2​A+B→4​A+4​B2A+B\to 4A+4B and 4​A+4​B→A4A+4B\to A, which increases the number of molecules of AA at each cycle. It follows that every state is transient, independently on the choice of positive rate constants. □\square

We now show how a slight modification of the previous example leads to a strongly endotactic network that explodes for any initial condition.

Example 3.2.

By modifying the reaction network in Example 3.1 we obtain

0→2​A→4​A+B→6​A+4​B→3​A.0\to 2A\to 4A+B\to 6A+4B\to 3A.

The network is still strongly endotactic, as can be checked by utilizing a similar techinque as in Example 3.1. Moreover, and similarly as in Example 3.1, it can be verified that from any state x∈ℤdx\in\mathbb{Z}^{d} it is possible to reach a state of the form x′=(xA′,0)x^{\prime}=(x^{\prime}_{A},0), and by letting the reaction 0→2​A0\to 2A take place we may assume that xA′≥2x^{\prime}_{A}\geq 2. There is then a positive probability that starting from x′x^{\prime} the infinite repetition of the sequence of reactions 2​A→4​A+B2A\to 4A+B, 4​A+B→6​A+4​B4A+B\to 6A+4B, and 6​A+4​B→3​A6A+4B\to 3A occurs, each cycle increasing the number of molecules of AA by 1. The main difference with the previous example is that by the monotone convergence theorem the expected time it takes for the infinite repetition of the reaction sequence 2​A→4​A+B2A\to 4A+B, 4​A+B→6​A+4​B4A+B\to 6A+4B, and 6​A+4​B→3​A6A+4B\to 3A to take place, m⁡(xA′)m(x_{A}^{\prime}), is bounded by

m(xA′)<∑n=xA′∞\displaystyle m(x^{\prime}_{A})<\sum_{n=x^{\prime}_{A}}^{\infty} (1κ2​A→4​A+B​n​(n−1)+1κ4​A+B→6​A+4​B​(n+2)​(n+1)​n​(n−1)CLOSE\displaystyle\Bigg(\frac{1}{\kappa_{2A\to 4A+B}n(n-1)}+\frac{1}{\kappa_{4A+B\to 6A+4B}(n+2)(n+1)n(n-1)}
OPEN+1κ6​A+4​B→3​A​(n+4)​(n+3)​(n+2)​(n+1)​n​(n−1)⋅4!)<∞,\displaystyle+\frac{1}{\kappa_{6A+4B\to 3A}(n+4)(n+3)(n+2)(n+1)n(n-1)\cdot 4!}\Bigg)<\infty,

so the model is explosive [33]. For more on explosive stochastic reaction networks, see [6]. □\square

We provide an example that is not strongly endotactic. This model will be considered in Remark 4.4.

Example 3.3.

The reaction network

A⇌2​B,A+C⇌B+CA\rightleftharpoons 2B,\quad A+C\rightleftharpoons B+C

is not strongly endotactic. Indeed, consider the vector w=(1,1,10)w=(1,1,10): it is not orthogonal to the stoichiometric subspace since ⟨w,(−1,2,0)⟩≠0\langle w,(-1,2,0)\rangle\neq 0, (−1,2,0)(-1,2,0) being the reaction vector of A→2​BA\to 2B. It can be checked that the w−w-maximal complexes are A+CA+C and B+CB+C, but there is no reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} with y∈{A+C,B+C}y\in\{A+C,B+C\} and ⟨w,y′−y⟩<0\langle w,y^{\prime}-y\rangle<0.

It is interesting to note that within every stoichiometric compatibility class the amount of molecules of CC is kept constant, hence the above network equipped with mass-action kinetics is equivalent to

B⇌A⇌2​B,B\rightleftharpoons A\rightleftharpoons 2B,

for a suitable choice of rate constants. Somewhat surprisingly, the latter is strongly endotactic by Proposition 3.1. □\square

4 Tiers

This section is broken into 3 subsections. In subsection 4.1, we introduce the relevant definitions related to tiers. We also provide a few results related to these definitions. In subsection 4.2, we provide Theorem 4.2, which is our main technical result and characterizes strongly endotactic networks in terms of their tier structures. Finally, in subsection 4.3, we collect results relating tier sequences with a commonly used Lyapunov function that plays a role in each of the subsequent results of the present paper.

4.1 Definitions

Definition 4.1.

A sequence (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} of positive vectors of ℝ>0d\mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0} is called a tier sequence if

limn→∞‖ln⁡(xn)‖∞=∞\lim_{n\to\infty}\|\ln(x_{n})\|_{\infty}=\infty

and for all pairs of complexes y,y′∈𝒞y,y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C} the limit

limn→∞xny′−y\lim_{n\to\infty}x_{n}^{y^{\prime}-y}

exists (it could be infinity). Moreover, a tier sequence is proper if for all n,m∈ℤ≥0n,m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} we have xn−xm∈Sx_{n}-x_{m}\in S.

Remark 4.1.

Note that, given a sequence (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} of positive vectors in ℝ>0d\mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0} with limn→∞‖ln⁡(xn)‖∞=∞\lim_{n\to\infty}\|\ln(x_{n})\|_{\infty}=\infty, it is always possible to extract a subsequence that is a tier sequence. This follows from the fact that there are finitely many complexes.

Remark 4.2.

The definition of tier sequence is tied to the choice of mass action kinetics for the reaction network. Indeed, xnyx_{n}^{y} is proportional to the deterministic mass action rate function associated with a reaction whose source is yy, and xny−y′x_{n}^{y-y^{\prime}} is nothing but the ratio xny/xny′x_{n}^{y}/x_{n}^{y^{\prime}}. Hence, a sequence is a tier sequence if a ranking of the reaction rates λD\lambda^{D} along xnx_{n} can be made, in the sense specified by the next definition. We also note here that the focus of this paper will be on the relative behavior of reaction rate functions along sequences diverging to infinity, with the aim to understand the behavior of the dynamics of the associated reaction network. Since the stoichiometric compatibility classes are invariant sets for both the deterministic and the stochastic models, it makes sense to restrict our analysis to proper tier sequences.

Definition 4.2.

Given a tier sequence (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty}, we define tiers as subsets of 𝒞\mathcal{C} in the following recursive manner:

  1. 1.

    we say that a complex yy is in tier 1 (and write y∈T(xn)1y\in T^{1}_{(x_{n})}) if for all complexes y′∈𝒞y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}

    limn→∞xny−y′>0;\lim_{n\to\infty}x_{n}^{y-y^{\prime}}>0;
  2. 2.

    we say that a complex yy is in tier ii (and write y∈T(xn)iy\in T^{i}_{(x_{n})}) if there exists y′∈T(xn)i−1y^{\prime}\in T^{i-1}_{(x_{n})} with

    limn→∞xny−y′=0\lim_{n\to\infty}x_{n}^{y-y^{\prime}}=0

    and for all complexes y′∉⋃j=1i−1T(xn)jy^{\prime}\notin\bigcup_{j=1}^{i-1}T^{j}_{(x_{n})} we have

    limn→∞xny−y′>0.\lim_{n\to\infty}x_{n}^{y-y^{\prime}}>0.

Given a tier sequence, tiers describe a partition of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. We further define an order relation on 𝒞\mathcal{C} in the following way: we write y≾(xn)y′y\precsim_{(x_{n})}y^{\prime} if y∈T(xn)iy\in T^{i}_{(x_{n})}, y′∈T(xn)jy^{\prime}\in T^{j}_{(x_{n})} and i≥ji\geq j. Similarly, we write y≺(xn)y′y\prec_{(x_{n})}y^{\prime} if y∈T(xn)iy\in T^{i}_{(x_{n})}, y′∈T(xn)jy^{\prime}\in T^{j}_{(x_{n})} and i>ji>j. Note that the inequality on the indexes of the tiers is reversed, and y≺(xn)y′y\prec_{(x_{n})}y^{\prime} if and only if the ratio xny/xny′x_{n}^{y}/x_{n}^{y^{\prime}} converges to 0 as nn tends to infinity, meaning that xnyx_{n}^{y} is much smaller than xny′x_{n}^{y^{\prime}} for large nn. Finally, we write y∼(xn)y′y\sim_{(x_{n})}y^{\prime} if yy and y′y^{\prime} are in the same tier. Note that by definition for all complexes y∈𝒞y\in\mathcal{C} we have y∼(xn)yy\sim_{(x_{n})}y.

Definition 4.3.

We say that a tier sequence (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is transversal if there exists at least one reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} such that

limn→∞|ln⁡(xny′−y)|=∞.\lim_{n\to\infty}|\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\prime}-y})|=\infty.
Remark 4.3.

Equivalently, transversal tier sequences can be defined as those tier sequences for which there exists y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} such that the complexes yy and y′y^{\prime} are in different tiers. These reactions will play an important role in the proofs of our results. We will prove in Lemma 4.1 that all proper tier sequences (which are those we will focus on, see Remark 4.2) are transversal.

Example 4.1.

Consider the reaction network

A⇌B⇌2​CA\rightleftharpoons B\rightleftharpoons 2C

and the sequences (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} and (x^n)n=0∞(\hat{x}_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} defined by

xn=(1n,5−1n−12​n,1n)andx^n=(en,2​en,1n).x_{n}=\left(\frac{1}{n},5-\frac{1}{n}-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{n}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad\hat{x}_{n}=\left(e^{n},2e^{n},\frac{1}{n}\right).

Then, (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is a proper tier sequence, which we demonstrate now. The entries xn,1x_{n,1} and xn,3x_{n,3} go to zero as nn goes to infinity, which implies limn→∞‖ln⁡(xn)‖∞=∞\lim_{n\to\infty}\|\ln(x_{n})\|_{\infty}=\infty. Moreover,

limn→∞xn(−1,0,2)=1andlimn→∞xn(−1,1,0)=∞,\lim_{n\to\infty}x_{n}^{(-1,0,2)}=1\quad\text{and}\quad\lim_{n\to\infty}x_{n}^{(-1,1,0)}=\infty,

which implies that (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is a tier sequence and A∼(xn)2CA\sim_{(x_{n})}2C and A≺(xn)BA\prec_{(x_{n})}B. Finally, (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is proper because for any n≥1n\geq 1

xn+1−xn=(1n+1−1n)​(1,−1,0)+(12​n+1−12​n)​(0,−1,2)∈S.x_{n+1}-x_{n}=\left(\frac{1}{n+1}-\frac{1}{n}\right)(1,-1,0)+\left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{n+1}}-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{n}}\right)(0,-1,2)\in S.

For what concerns (x^n)n=0∞(\hat{x}_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty}, we still have limn→∞‖ln⁡(x^n)‖∞=∞\lim_{n\to\infty}\|\ln(\hat{x}_{n})\|_{\infty}=\infty. Moreover,

limn→∞x^n(0,−1,2)=0andlimn→∞xn(−1,1,0)=2,\lim_{n\to\infty}\hat{x}_{n}^{(0,-1,2)}=0\quad\text{and}\quad\lim_{n\to\infty}x_{n}^{(-1,1,0)}=2,

so (x^n)n=0∞(\hat{x}_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is a tier sequence and A∼(x^n)BA\sim_{(\hat{x}_{n})}B and 2C≺(x^n)A2C\prec_{(\hat{x}_{n})}A. Finally, (x^n)n=0∞(\hat{x}_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is transversal but not proper, indeed

limn→∞|ln⁡(x^n(0,−1,2))|=∞\lim_{n\to\infty}|\ln(\hat{x}_{n}^{(0,-1,2)})|=\infty

but for any n≥1n\geq 1

⟨x^n+1−x^n,(2,−2,1)⟩=−2​(en+1−en)+1n+1−1n≠0,\langle\hat{x}_{n+1}-\hat{x}_{n},(2,-2,1)\rangle=-2(e^{n+1}-e^{n})+\frac{1}{n+1}-\frac{1}{n}\neq 0,

and (2,−2,1)(2,-2,1) is orthogonal to SS (hence x^n+1−x^n∉S\hat{x}_{n+1}-\hat{x}_{n}\notin S). □\square

The following result connects proper and transversal tier sequences. As illustrated in Example 4.1, the converse does not hold.

Lemma 4.1.

A proper tier sequence is transversal.

Proof.

Consider a proper tier sequence (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty}. By definition,

limn→∞‖ln⁡(xn)‖∞=∞\lim_{n\to\infty}\|\ln(x_{n})\|_{\infty}=\infty

and

limn→∞|ln⁡(xny′−y)|\lim_{n\to\infty}|\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\prime}-y})|

exists for any y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}. After potentially considering a subsequence, we may assume that for any n≥0n\geq 0

xn+1,i≥xn,i\displaystyle x_{n+1,i}\geq x_{n,i} if ​lim supn→∞ln⁡(xn,i)=∞;\displaystyle\quad\text{if }\limsup_{n\to\infty}\ln(x_{n,i})=\infty;
xn+1,i≤xn,i\displaystyle x_{n+1,i}\leq x_{n,i} if ​lim infn→∞ln⁡(xn,i)=−∞,\displaystyle\quad\text{if }\liminf_{n\to\infty}\ln(x_{n,i})=-\infty,

which implies that the above lim sup\limsup and lim inf\liminf are limits. It also follows that

limn→∞|ln⁡(xn,i)|=∞\lim_{n\to\infty}|\ln(x_{n,i})|=\infty

for at least one index 1≤i≤d1\leq i\leq d. Hence, by [4, Theorem 3.9] there exists a vector w∈ℝdw\in\mathbb{R}^{d} such that

wi>0\displaystyle w_{i}>0 if and only if ​limn→∞ln⁡(xn,i)=∞;\displaystyle\quad\text{if and only if }\lim_{n\to\infty}\ln(x_{n,i})=\infty;
wi<0\displaystyle w_{i}<0 if and only if ​limn→∞ln⁡(xn,i)=−∞;\displaystyle\quad\text{if and only if }\lim_{n\to\infty}\ln(x_{n,i})=-\infty;
⟨w,y′−y⟩=0\displaystyle\langle w,y^{\prime}-y\rangle=0 if y∼(xn)y′.\displaystyle\quad\text{if }y\sim_{(x_{n})}y^{\prime}.

Note that wi=0w_{i}=0 if lim supn→∞|ln⁡(xn,i)|<∞\limsup_{n\to\infty}|\ln(x_{n,i})|<\infty. In particular, it follows that

limn→∞⟨w,xn⟩={∞if ​limn→∞‖xn‖∞=∞;0otherwise.\lim_{n\to\infty}\langle w,x_{n}\rangle=\begin{cases}\infty&\text{if }\lim_{n\to\infty}\|x_{n}\|_{\infty}=\infty;\\ 0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}.

We will show that there must be an n^≥1\hat{n}\geq 1 for which ⟨w,xn^⟩≠0\langle w,x_{\hat{n}}\rangle\neq 0. First, if limn→∞⟨w,xn⟩=∞\lim_{n\to\infty}\langle w,x_{n}\rangle=\infty, the assertion is clear. If, on the other hand, limn→∞⟨w,xn⟩=0\lim_{n\to\infty}\langle w,x_{n}\rangle=0, then none of the xn,ix_{n,i} converge to infinity. Since all the vectors {xn}n=0∞\{x_{n}\}_{n=0}^{\infty} are positive, and at least one of xn,ix_{n,i} converges to zero, we may conclude that ⟨w,xn⟩<0\langle w,x_{n}\rangle<0 for all nn.

If (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} were not transversal, then we would have

limn→∞|ln⁡(xny′−y)|<∞\lim_{n\to\infty}|\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\prime}-y})|<\infty

for any reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}, which would imply that y∼(xn)y′y\sim_{(x_{n})}y^{\prime} for any y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}. It would follow that ⟨w,y′−y⟩=0\langle w,y^{\prime}-y\rangle=0 for any y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}, which means w∈S⟂w\in S^{\perp}. Let n^≥1\hat{n}\geq 1 be such that ⟨w,xn^⟩≠0\langle w,x_{\hat{n}}\rangle\neq 0. Since (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is proper, we have

limn→∞⟨w,xn⟩=⟨w,xn^⟩+limn→∞⟨w,xn−xn^⟩=⟨w,xn^⟩∉{0,∞}.\lim_{n\to\infty}\langle w,x_{n}\rangle=\langle w,x_{\hat{n}}\rangle+\lim_{n\to\infty}\langle w,x_{n}-x_{\hat{n}}\rangle=\langle w,x_{\hat{n}}\rangle\notin\{0,\infty\}.

This is a contradiction, and the proof is concluded. ∎

For notational convenience, we give the following definition.

Definition 4.4.

Define 𝒞S⊆𝒞\mathcal{C}^{S}\subseteq\mathcal{C} to be the set of source complexes. Given a tier sequence (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty}, we define source tier 1 to be the set

T(xn)1,S={y∈𝒞S:y′≾(xn)y for all y′∈𝒞S}.T^{1,S}_{(x_{n})}=\{y\in\mathcal{C}^{S}\,:\,y^{\prime}\precsim_{(x_{n})}y\text{ for all }y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}^{S}\}.

The following is a key concept of this paper, and will provide a characterization of strongly endotactic networks.

Definition 4.5.

We say that a tier sequence (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is tier descending if both the following statements hold:

  1. 1.

    for all y∈T(xn)1,Sy\in T^{1,S}_{(x_{n})} and all y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} we have y′≾(xn)yy^{\prime}\precsim_{(x_{n})}y;

  2. 2.

    there exist y∈T(xn)1,Sy\in T^{1,S}_{(x_{n})} and y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} with y′≺(xn)yy^{\prime}\prec_{(x_{n})}y.

Moreover, we say that a reaction network 𝒢\mathcal{G} is tier descending if all transversal tier sequences are tier descending.

4.2 Relation between strongly endotactic networks and its tiers

We now state our first main result, which provides a characterization of strongly endotactic networks in terms of tiers.

Theorem 4.2.

A reaction network is strongly endotactic if and only if it is tier descending.

Before proceeding with the proof of Theorem 4.2, we present an immediate corollary.

Corollary 4.3.

If a reaction network is strongly endotactic, then every proper tier sequence is tier descending. Moreover, if S=ℝdS=\mathbb{R}^{d} then a reaction network is strongly endotactic if and only if every proper tier sequence is tier descending.

Proof.

The first part of the result follows from Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 4.2. Moreover, if S=ℝdS=\mathbb{R}^{d} then any transversal tier sequence is proper (since all sequences are proper in this case), and the proof follows from Theorem 4.2. ∎

Remark 4.4.

It is tempting to believe that if every proper tier sequence of a reaction network is tier descending, then the network is strongly endotactic. By Corollary 4.3 we see that this is true in the case when S=ℝdS=\mathbb{R}^{d}. However, this statement is false, in general. As an example, consider the reaction network

A⇌2​B,A+C⇌B+C.A\rightleftharpoons 2B,\quad A+C\rightleftharpoons B+C.

The network is not strongly endotactic, as shown in Example 3.3. Nevertheless, every proper tier sequence is tier descending: since no reaction changes the amount of molecules of the species CC, every proper tier sequence (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is of the form

xn=(xn,1,xn,2,c)x_{n}=(x_{n,1},x_{n,2},c)

for a constant c∈ℝ>0c\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}. It is then easy to check that (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is tier descending if and only if (x^n)n=0∞(\hat{x}_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} defined by

x^n=(xn,1,xn,2)\hat{x}_{n}=(x_{n,1},x_{n,2})

is tier descending for

B⇌A⇌2​B.B\rightleftharpoons A\rightleftharpoons 2B.

The latter is strongly endotactic by Proposition 3.1. Hence, each proper tier sequence (such as (x^n)n=0∞(\hat{x}_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty}) is tier descending by Corollary 4.3, thus proving our claim.

We now proceed by providing a key lemma that will be used in the proof of Theorem 4.2.

Lemma 4.4.

If (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is a tier sequence, then there exist ℓ∈ℤ\ell\in\mathbb{Z} with 0<ℓ≤d0<\ell\leq d, sequences of positive real numbers (mn1)n=0∞(m^{1}_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty}, (mn2)n=0∞(m^{2}_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty}, …\dots, (mnℓ)n=0∞(m^{\ell}_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty}, a sequence of real vectors (Cn)n=0∞(C_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty}, vectors α1,α2,…,αℓ∈ℝd\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\dots,\alpha_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and a subsequence (xnk)k=0∞(x_{n_{k}})_{k=0}^{\infty} such that:

  1. 1.

    ln⁡(xnk)=∑i=1ℓmnki​αi+Cnk\ln(x_{n_{k}})=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}m^{i}_{n_{k}}\alpha_{i}+C_{n_{k}};

  2. 2.

    lim supk→∞‖Cnk‖∞<∞\limsup_{k\to\infty}\|C_{n_{k}}\|_{\infty}<\infty;

  3. 3.

    For all 1≤i≤ℓ1\leq i\leq\ell we have limk→∞mnki=∞\lim_{k\to\infty}m^{i}_{n_{k}}=\infty, and if 1≤j<i≤ℓ1\leq j<i\leq\ell then limk→∞mnki/mnkj=0\lim_{k\to\infty}m^{i}_{n_{k}}/m^{j}_{n_{k}}=0;

  4. 4.

    if y′∼(xn)yy^{\prime}\sim_{(x_{n})}y then ⟨y′−y,αi⟩=0\langle y^{\prime}-y,\alpha_{i}\rangle=0 for all 1≤i≤ℓ1\leq i\leq\ell;

    if y′≺(xn)yy^{\prime}\prec_{(x_{n})}y then

    iy,y′=min⁡{1≤i≤ℓ:⟨αi,y′−y⟩≠0}i_{y,y^{\prime}}=\min\{1\leq i\leq\ell\,:\,\langle\alpha_{i},y^{\prime}-y\rangle\neq 0\} (4.1)

    exists and ⟨αiy,y′,y′−y⟩<0\langle\alpha_{i_{y,y^{\prime}}},y^{\prime}-y\rangle<0.

Remark 4.5.

Parts 1 and 2 of the lemma show that the logarithm of a tier sequence can be substantially decomposed into fixed vectors, αi\alpha_{i}, apart from a bounded error term, CnkC_{n_{k}}. Part 3 then shows that if i<ji<j, then the influence of the vector αi\alpha_{i} is greater than the influence of the vector αj\alpha_{j}. Finally, by parts 4 and 5 we see that the αi\alpha_{i}’s separate complexes in a natural manner among the tiers.

As an example, consider the reaction network

A⇌B⇌2​CA\rightleftharpoons B\rightleftharpoons 2C

and the tier sequence

xn=(1n,5−1n−12​n,1n),x_{n}=\left(\frac{1}{n},5-\frac{1}{n}-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{n}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\right),

introduced in Example 4.1. We have

ln⁡(xnk)=ln⁡(n)​(−1,0,−12)+Cn,\ln(x_{n_{k}})=\ln(n)\left(-1,0,-\frac{1}{2}\right)+C_{n},

where

Cn=(0,ln⁡(5−1n−12​n),0).C_{n}=\left(0,\ln\left(5-\frac{1}{n}-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{n}}\right),0\right).

Note that ‖Cn‖∞<ln⁡(5)\|C_{n}\|_{\infty}<\ln(5) for all n>1n>1. Moreover, recall that A∼(xn)2CA\sim_{(x_{n})}2C and A≺(xn)BA\prec_{(x_{n})}B, which is implied also by parts 4 and 5 of the lemma, since

⟨(1,0,−2),(−1,0,−12)⟩=0and⟨(1,−1,0),(−1,0,−12)⟩<0.\left\langle(1,0,-2),\left(-1,0,-\frac{1}{2}\right)\right\rangle=0\quad\text{and}\quad\left\langle(1,-1,0),\left(-1,0,-\frac{1}{2}\right)\right\rangle<0.
Proof of Lemma 4.4.

Define mn1=‖ln⁡(xn)‖∞m^{1}_{n}=\|\ln(x_{n})\|_{\infty}. Note that for any n≥0n\geq 0 we have ‖ln⁡(xn)/mn1‖∞=1\|\ln(x_{n})/m^{1}_{n}\|_{\infty}=1. Hence, we can consider a subsequence of (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} such that

This implies that at least one entry of ln⁡(xnk)\ln(x_{n_{k}}) has absolute value constantly equal to mnk1m^{1}_{n_{k}}. then define mnkj=‖ln⁡(xnk)−∑i=1j−1mnki​αi‖∞m^{j}_{n_{k}}=\|\ln(x_{n_{k}})-\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}m^{i}_{n_{k}}\alpha_{i}\|_{\infty}. By potentially considering a subsequence of (xnk)k=0∞(x_{n_{k}})_{k=0}^{\infty}, we can assume that

Moreover, we can choose a subsequence such that the maximal absolute values of the entries of ln⁡(xnk)−∑i=1j−1mnki​αi\ln(x_{n_{k}})-\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}m^{i}_{n_{k}}\alpha_{i} are always obtained in the same position, so by induction it follows that at least j−1j-1 components of ln⁡(xnk)−∑i=1j−1mnki​αi\ln(x_{n_{k}})-\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}m^{i}_{n_{k}}\alpha_{i} are equal to zero for kk large enough (the argument is the same as for j=1j=1, which serves as base case). Now we are able to prove Theorem 4.2.

Proof of Theorem 4.2.

Assume that the network is tier descending. Consider a vector ww that is not orthogonal to the stoichiometric subspace SS. Consider the sequence (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} defined by

(4.4)

Hence, (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is a tier sequence. It follows that (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is tier descending, which together with equation 4.4 concludes the proof of one direction of the result.

For the other direction, we suppose that the network is strongly endotactic. Let (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} be a transversal tier sequence. In order to prove the result, it is sufficient to construct a vector ww such that

Note that (xnk)k=0∞(x_{n_{k}})_{k=0}^{\infty} is still a transversal tier sequence, and the tier structures of (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} and of its subsequence (xnk)k=0∞(x_{n_{k}})_{k=0}^{\infty} are identical, meaning that for any i≥1i\geq 1 we have T(xn)i=T(xnk)iT^{i}_{(x_{n})}=T^{i}_{(x_{n_{k}})}. 4.3 Tier sequences and Lyapunov functions

Let u⁡(x):ℝ→ℝ≥0u(x):\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be the function

u⁡(x)={x⁡(ln⁡x−1)+1ifx>0,1otherwise.\displaystyle u(x)=\begin{cases}x(\ln{x}-1)+1\quad&\text{if}\quad x>0,\\ 1\quad&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (4.5)

Then we define

U⁡(x)=1+∑i=1du⁡(xi).U(x)=1+\sum_{i=1}^{d}u(x_{i}). (4.6)

This function has been utilized often as a Lyapunov function in the context of reaction network theory. In particular, it was utilized in the foundational papers of the field in order prove local asympotic stability of complex balanced deterministic mass action systems [20, 25]. Moreover, it (or slight modifications thereof) has notably been used to derive the results of [5, 4, 24, 2], which are of direct interest for the present paper. More discussion on the role of Lyapunov functions for stochastic reaction networks can be found in [8] and [10].

In the present section, we will unveil some important connections between tier sequences and the Lyapunov function (4.6) by extending the techniques of [5] to the setting of tier descending networks. We will then use these connections to develop the results presented in sections 5, 6, and 7.

Lemma 4.5.

Consider a tier descending reaction network 𝒢\mathcal{G} and let (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} be a transversal tier sequence. Then, for any y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} with y≾(xn)y′y\precsim_{(x_{n})}y^{\prime} there exists y⋆∈𝒞y^{\star}\in\mathcal{C} and y⋆→y⋆⁣⋆∈ℛy^{\star}\to y^{\star\star}\in\mathcal{R} such that y≾(xn)y⋆y\precsim_{(x_{n})}y^{\star}, y⋆⁣⋆≺(xn)y⋆y^{\star\star}\prec_{(x_{n})}y^{\star} and for any choice of c1,c2∈ℝ>0c_{1},c_{2}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} and c3,c4∈ℝc_{3},c_{4}\in\mathbb{R} there exists N<∞N<\infty with

c1​xny⋆​(ln⁡(xny⋆⁣⋆−y⋆)+c3)+c2​xny​(ln⁡(xny′−y)+c4)<0for all ​n≥N.c_{1}x_{n}^{y^{\star}}\left(\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\star\star}-y^{\star}})+c_{3}\right)+c_{2}x_{n}^{y}\left(\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\prime}-y})+c_{4}\right)<0\quad\text{for all }n\geq N. (4.7)

Moreover, if there exists a c∈ℝ>0c\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} for which xny⋆≥c>0x_{n}^{y^{\star}}\geq c>0 for all nn, then for any choice of c1,c2∈ℝ>0c_{1},c_{2}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} and c3,c4∈ℝc_{3},c_{4}\in\mathbb{R} we have

limn→∞(c1​xny⋆​(ln⁡(xny⋆⁣⋆−y⋆)+c3)+c2​xny​(ln⁡(xny′−y)+c4))=−∞.\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(c_{1}x_{n}^{y^{\star}}\left(\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\star\star}-y^{\star}})+c_{3}\right)+c_{2}x_{n}^{y}\left(\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\prime}-y})+c_{4}\right)\right)=-\infty. (4.8)
Proof.

Fix y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}. We consider two cases separately: y∼(xn)y′y\sim_{(x_{n})}y^{\prime} and y≺(xn)y′y\prec_{(x_{n})}y^{\prime}.

Case 1. Assume that y∼(xn)y′y\sim_{(x_{n})}y^{\prime}. Then

limn→∞|ln⁡(xny′−y)|<∞.\lim_{n\to\infty}|\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\prime}-y})|<\infty.

By the definition of a descending reaction network there must be at least one reaction y⋆→y⋆⁣⋆y^{\star}\to y^{\star\star} with y⋆∈T(xn)1,Sy^{\star}\in T^{1,S}_{(x_{n})} (implying y≾(xn)y⋆y\precsim_{(x_{n})}y^{\star}) and y⋆⁣⋆≺(xn)y⋆y^{\star\star}\prec_{(x_{n})}y^{\star}. Hence, we have

limn→∞xny−y⋆<∞\lim_{n\to\infty}x_{n}^{y-y^{\star}}<\infty

and

limn→∞ln⁡(xny⋆⁣⋆−y⋆)=−∞.\lim_{n\to\infty}\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\star\star}-y^{\star}})=-\infty.

It follows that

c1​xny⋆​(ln⁡(xny⋆⁣⋆−y⋆)CLOSE\displaystyle c_{1}x_{n}^{y^{\star}}\big(\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\star\star}-y^{\star}}) OPEN+c3)+c2​xny​(ln⁡(xny′−y)+c4)\displaystyle+c_{3}\big)+c_{2}x_{n}^{y}\big(\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\prime}-y})+c_{4}\big)
=xny⋆​(c1​(ln⁡(xny⋆⁣⋆−y⋆)+c3)+c2​xny−y⋆​(ln⁡(xny′−y)+c4))\displaystyle=x_{n}^{y^{\star}}\left(c_{1}\left(\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\star\star}-y^{\star}})+c_{3}\right)+c_{2}x_{n}^{y-y^{\star}}\left(\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\prime}-y})+c_{4}\right)\right)

is negative for nn large enough, which proves (4.7). Moreover, if xny⋆≥c>0x_{n}^{y^{\star}}\geq c>0, then (4.8) follows.

Case 2. We prove the result by contradiction. Assume that y≺(xn)y′y\prec_{(x_{n})}y^{\prime}. If (4.7) did not hold, then there would exist a subsequence (xnk)k=0∞(x_{n_{k}})_{k=0}^{\infty} such that for any y⋆→y⋆⁣⋆∈ℛy^{\star}\to y^{\star\star}\in\mathcal{R} with y≾(xn)y⋆y\precsim_{(x_{n})}y^{\star} and y⋆⁣⋆≺(xn)y⋆y^{\star\star}\prec_{(x_{n})}y^{\star}, there exist c1,c2∈ℝ>0c_{1},c_{2}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} and c3,c4∈ℝc_{3},c_{4}\in\mathbb{R} with

c1​xny⋆​(ln⁡(xny⋆⁣⋆−y⋆)+c3)+c2​xny​(ln⁡(xny′−y)+c4)≥0for all ​k∈ℤ≥0.c_{1}x_{n}^{y^{\star}}\left(\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\star\star}-y^{\star}})+c_{3}\right)+c_{2}x_{n}^{y}\left(\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\prime}-y})+c_{4}\right)\geq 0\quad\text{for all }k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. (4.9)

Our aim is to prove that such a subsequence does not exist.

Every subsequence of a descending tier sequence is still a descending tier sequence. Hence, by potentially considering a further subsequence, we can assume that (xnk)k=0∞(x_{n_{k}})_{k=0}^{\infty} is as in Lemma 4.4.

Consider the sequence (x~nk)k=0∞(\tilde{x}_{n_{k}})_{k=0}^{\infty} defined by

ln⁡(x~nk)=∑i=1iy′,ymnki​αi\ln(\tilde{x}_{n_{k}})=\sum_{i=1}^{i_{y^{\prime},y}}m^{i}_{n_{k}}\alpha_{i} (4.10)

where iy′,yi_{y^{\prime},y} is as defined in (4.1), and exists by Lemma 4.4(5). We will first show that (x~nk)k=0∞(\tilde{x}_{n_{k}})_{k=0}^{\infty} is also a transversal tier sequence, and is therefore tier descending. We then prove that there exist y⋆∈𝒞y^{\star}\in\mathcal{C} and y⋆→y⋆⁣⋆∈ℛy^{\star}\to y^{\star\star}\in\mathcal{R} such that y≺(x~nk)y⋆y\prec_{(\tilde{x}_{n_{k}})}y^{\star}, y⋆⁣⋆≺(x~nk)y⋆y^{\star\star}\prec_{(\tilde{x}_{n_{k}})}y^{\star}. Finally, we will prove that these complex orderings are valid also when considerering the original tier sequence (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty}, as required by the lemma.

By Lemma 4.4(3), we have

limk→∞‖ln⁡(x~nk)‖∞mnk1​‖α1‖∞=1,\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{\left\|\ln(\tilde{x}_{n_{k}})\right\|_{\infty}}{m_{n_{k}}^{1}\left\|\alpha_{1}\right\|_{\infty}}=1,

and so limk→∞‖ln⁡(x~nk)‖∞=∞\lim_{k\to\infty}\|\ln(\tilde{x}_{n_{k}})\|_{\infty}=\infty. Furthermore, for any two complexes y~,y~′∈𝒞\tilde{y},\tilde{y}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C} the limit

limk→∞x~nky~′−y~=limk→∞e∑i=1iy′,ymnki​⟨αi,y~′−y~⟩\lim_{k\to\infty}\tilde{x}_{n_{k}}^{\tilde{y}^{\prime}-\tilde{y}}=\lim_{k\to\infty}e^{\sum_{i=1}^{i_{y^{\prime},y}}m^{i}_{n_{k}}\langle\alpha_{i},\tilde{y}^{\prime}-\tilde{y}\rangle}

exists (it can potentially be infinity). Hence, (x~nk)k=0∞(\tilde{x}_{n_{k}})_{k=0}^{\infty} is a tier sequence. Moreover,

limk→∞|ln⁡(x~nky′−y)|=limk→∞|∑i=1iy′,ymnki​⟨αi,y′−y⟩|=limk→∞mnkiy′,y​|⟨αiy′,y,y′−y⟩|=∞.\lim_{k\to\infty}|\ln(\tilde{x}_{n_{k}}^{y^{\prime}-y})|=\lim_{k\to\infty}\left|\sum_{i=1}^{i_{y^{\prime},y}}m_{n_{k}}^{i}\langle\alpha_{i},y^{\prime}-y\rangle\right|=\lim_{k\to\infty}m^{i_{y^{\prime},y}}_{n_{k}}|\langle\alpha_{i_{y^{\prime},y}},y^{\prime}-y\rangle|=\infty.

Hence, (x~nk)k=0∞(\tilde{x}_{n_{k}})_{k=0}^{\infty} is a transversal tier sequence. Since (x~nk)k=0∞(\tilde{x}_{n_{k}})_{k=0}^{\infty} is a tier sequence, Lemma 4.4 guarantees that it can be decomposed as detailed therein.
