Proposition 4.6.

Consider a tier descending reaction network 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Then, for any transversal tier sequence (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} and any choice of positive constants κy→y′\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}, there exists N<∞N<\infty such that

∑y→y′∈ℛκy→y′​xny​ln⁡(xny′−y)<0for all ​n≥N.\sum_{y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}x_{n}^{y}\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\prime}-y})<0\quad\text{for all }n\geq N. (4.16)

Moreover, if the complex 0 is a source complex, then

limn→∞∑y→y′∈ℛκy→y′​xny​ln⁡(xny′−y)=−∞.\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}x_{n}^{y}\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\prime}-y})=-\infty. (4.17)
Proof.

The result follows from noting that for any reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} either y′≺(xn)yy^{\prime}\prec_{(x_{n})}y and

xny​ln⁡(xnky′−y)<0,x_{n}^{y}\ln(x_{n_{k}}^{y^{\prime}-y})<0,

or y≾(xn)y′y\precsim_{(x_{n})}y^{\prime} and Lemma 4.5 holds. Hence, since there are finitely many reactions, for any choice of positive constants κy→y′\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}} there exists N<∞N<\infty such that (4.16) holds.

For the second part of the statement, assume that 0 is a source complex. Then, by definition of T(xn)1,ST^{1,S}_{(x_{n})} we have 0≾(xn)y0\precsim_{(x_{n})}y for all y∈T(xn)1,Sy\in T^{1,S}_{(x_{n})}, which implies that for all y∈T(xn)1,Sy\in T^{1,S}_{(x_{n})}

limn→∞xny=limn→∞xny−0>0.\lim_{n\to\infty}x_{n}^{y}=\lim_{n\to\infty}x_{n}^{y-0}>0.

Since (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is transversal and 𝒢\mathcal{G} is tier descending, (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is tier descending. Hence, there is a reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} with y∈T(xn)1,Sy\in T^{1,S}_{(x_{n})} and y′≺(xn)yy^{\prime}\prec_{(x_{n})}y. Hence

limn→∞xny​ln⁡(xny′−y)=−∞,\lim_{n\to\infty}x_{n}^{y}\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\prime}-y})=-\infty,

and similarly as before (4.17) follows from Lemma 4.5. ∎

5 Persistence and Permanence

The paper [24] deals with persistence and permanence of deterministic mass action systems associated with a strongly endotactic reaction network. The relevant definitions are as follows.

Definition 5.1.

A deterministic reaction system is persistent if for any initial condition z⁡(0)∈ℝ>0dz(0)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0}

inft≥0zi​(t)>0for all ​1≤i≤d.\inf_{t\geq 0}z_{i}(t)>0\quad\text{for all }1\leq i\leq d.
Definition 5.2.

A deterministic reaction system is permanent if for every set

Sy=(y+S)∩ℝ>0dS_{y}=(y+S)\cap\mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0}

with y∈ℝ>0dy\in\mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0}, there exists a compact set K⊂SyK\subset S_{y} such that for any initial condition z⁡(0)∈Syz(0)\in S_{y}

inf{t≥0:z(s)∈Kfor all s≥t}<∞.\inf\{t\geq 0\,:\,z(s)\in K\quad\text{for all }s\geq t\}<\infty.

Thus, a deterministic reaction system is permament if there exists a compact set in the interior of each positive stoichiometric compatibility class that eventually attracts all the solutions with a positive initial condition in that stoichiometric compatibility class. Note that if a reaction network is permanent, then it is non-explosive and persistent.

The following is an important result in [24]. It is used to prove persistence and permanence of strongly endotactic networks. In our setting, it can be derived as a corollary of the results on tier sequences stated in Section 4.3.

Corollary 5.1.

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be a strongly endotactic reaction network and consider a generalization of mass action kinetics with parameter dependent and time variable rate constants:

λy→y′​(x,t,θ)=κy→y′​(t,θ)​xy,\lambda_{y\to y^{\prime}}(x,t,\theta)=\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t,\theta)x^{y},

where θ\theta is in some parameter space Ω\Omega and t∈ℝ≥0t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}. Assume that there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that

δ<κy→y′​(t,θ)<1δfor all ​t≥0,θ∈Ω,y→y′∈ℛ.\delta<\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t,\theta)<\frac{1}{\delta}\quad\text{for all }t\geq 0,\theta\in\Omega,y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}. (5.1)

Let

z⁡(t,θ)=z⁡(0,θ)+∑y→y′∈ℛ(y′−y)​∫0tλy→y′​(z⁡(s,θ),s,θ)​𝑑s.z(t,\theta)=z(0,\theta)+\sum_{y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}(y^{\prime}-y)\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{y\to y^{\prime}}(z(s,\theta),s,\theta)\,ds.

Fix a set SyS_{y} as in Definition 5.2. Then, there exists a compact set Γ⊂Sy\Gamma\subset S_{y} such that

dd​t​U​(z⁡(t,θ))<0if ​z​(t,θ)∉Γ,\frac{d}{dt}U(z(t,\theta))<0\quad\text{if }z(t,\theta)\notin\Gamma,

given that z⁡(0,θ)∈Syz(0,\theta)\in S_{y} and U⁡(⋅)U(\cdot) is as in (4.6). In particular, it follows that for any open set BB containing the origin,

infz⁡(0,θ)∈ℝ>0d∖Binft≥0‖z⁡(t,θ)‖∞>0.\inf_{z(0,\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0}\setminus B}\inf_{t\geq 0}\|z(t,\theta)\|_{\infty}>0.
Proof.

If the result were not true, there would be a sequence of vectors (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} in SyS_{y} for which limn→∞‖ln⁡(xn)‖∞=∞\lim_{n\to\infty}\|\ln(x_{n})\|_{\infty}=\infty and an increasing sequence of times (tn)n=0∞(t_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} such that

∑y→y′∈ℛκy→y′​(tn)​xny​⟨y′−y,∇U​(xn)⟩=∑y→y′∈ℛκy→y′​(tn)​xny​ln⁡(xny′−y)≥0,\sum_{y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t_{n})x_{n}^{y}\langle y^{\prime}-y,\nabla U(x_{n})\rangle=\sum_{y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t_{n})x_{n}^{y}\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\prime}-y})\geq 0, (5.2)

for all n≥0n\geq 0. However, by Remark 4.1 we can extract a proper tier sequence from (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty}, hence (5.2) cannot hold by (5.1), Proposition 4.6 and Lemma 4.1.

The second part of the result follows by noting that the origin is a local maximum for the function U⁡(⋅)U(\cdot), and it is not contained in the compact set Γ\Gamma. Hence, for any open set BB (relative to ℝ≥0d\mathbb{R}^{d}_{\geq 0}) that contains the origin, there exists a neighborhood B′⊆BB^{\prime}\subseteq B of the origin (relative to ℝ≥0d\mathbb{R}^{d}_{\geq 0}) that does not intersect Γ\Gamma (implying that U⁡(z⁡(t,θ))U(z(t,\theta)) decreases if z⁡(t,θ)z(t,\theta) is in B′B^{\prime}), and such that

0=arg​maxx∈B′⁡U​(x).0=\argmax_{x\in B^{\prime}}U(x).

Hence, there exists an open set B′′B^{\prime\prime} (relative to ℝ≥0d\mathbb{R}^{d}_{\geq 0}) that contains the origin and cannot be reached by any trajectory with z⁡(0)∈ℝ>0d∖Bz(0)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0}\setminus B. ∎

We will also need the following results.

Lemma 5.2.

Assume that 𝒢\mathcal{G} is strongly endotactic, and consider a non-empty subset of species 𝒮~⊆𝒮\tilde{\mathcal{S}}\subseteq\mathcal{S}. Let pp be the projection from ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} onto the coordinates relative to the species in 𝒮~\tilde{\mathcal{S}}. Then, the reaction network 𝒢~=(𝒮~,𝒞~,ℛ~)\tilde{\mathcal{G}}=(\tilde{\mathcal{S}},\tilde{\mathcal{C}},\tilde{\mathcal{R}}) with

𝒞~\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{C}} ={p⁡(y):y∈𝒞}\displaystyle=\{p(y)\,:\,y\in\mathcal{C}\}
ℛ~\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{R}} ={p(y)→p(y′):y→y′∈ℛandp(y)≠p(y′)}\displaystyle=\{p(y)\to p(y^{\prime})\,:\,y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}\quad\text{and}\quad p(y)\neq p(y^{\prime})\}

is strongly endotactic.

Proof.

Let d~\tilde{d} be the cardinality of 𝒮~\tilde{\mathcal{S}}. For convenience, assume without loss of generality that the species of 𝒮~\tilde{\mathcal{S}} are ordered as the first d~\tilde{d} species, such that for any x∈ℝ≥0dx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}_{\geq 0} we can write x=(x~,x^)x=(\tilde{x},\hat{x}) with p⁡(x)=x~p(x)=\tilde{x} and x^∈ℝ≥0d−d~\hat{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d-\tilde{d}}_{\geq 0}. Let (x~n)n=0∞(\tilde{x}_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} be a transversal tier sequence of 𝒢~\tilde{\mathcal{G}}, fix x^∈ℝ>0d−d~\hat{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d-\tilde{d}}_{>0} and for any n≥0n\geq 0 let xn=(x~n,x^)x_{n}=(\tilde{x}_{n},\hat{x}). Note that for any n≥0n\geq 0 and for any complex y∈𝒞y\in\mathcal{C}, xnyx_{n}^{y} is equal to x~np⁡(y)\tilde{x}_{n}^{p(y)} times a multiplicative constant that is independent of nn. It follows that (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is a transversal tier sequence of 𝒢\mathcal{G}, and that for any i≥1i\geq 1 we have y∈T(xn)iy\in T^{i}_{(x_{n})} if and only if p⁡(y)∈T(x~n)ip(y)\in T^{i}_{(\tilde{x}_{n})}, which in turn implies that (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is tier descending if and only if (x~n)n=0∞(\tilde{x}_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is tier descending. Hence, we conclude that 𝒢~\tilde{\mathcal{G}} is strongly endotactic by the fact that 𝒢\mathcal{G} is strongly endotactic and by Theorem 4.2. ∎

Lemma 5.3.

Consider a deterministic mass action system (𝒢,Λ)(\mathcal{G},\Lambda), and assume 𝒢\mathcal{G} is strongly endotactic. Then, for any compact set Υ⊂ℝ>0d\Upsilon\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0}

supz⁡(0)∈Υsupt≥0‖z⁡(t)‖∞<∞\displaystyle\sup_{z(0)\in\Upsilon}\sup_{t\geq 0}\|z(t)\|_{\infty}<\infty (5.3)
infz⁡(0)∈Υinft≥0zi​(t)>0for all ​1≤i≤d.\displaystyle\inf_{z(0)\in\Upsilon}\inf_{t\geq 0}z_{i}(t)>0\quad\text{for all }1\leq i\leq d. (5.4)
Proof.

By Corollary 5.1, we have that there exists a compact set Γ⊂ℝ>0d\Gamma\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0} such that the function U⁡(z⁡(t))U(z(t)) is decreasing whenever z⁡(t)∉Γz(t)\notin\Gamma. It follows that

supz⁡(0)∈Υsupt≥0U⁡(z⁡(t))≤max⁡{maxz⁡(0)∈Υ⁡U⁡(z⁡(0)),maxx∈Γ⁡U⁡(x)}<∞,\sup_{z(0)\in\Upsilon}\sup_{t\geq 0}U(z(t))\leq\max\left\{\max_{z(0)\in\Upsilon}U(z(0)),\max_{x\in\Gamma}U(x)\right\}<\infty,

and the sets of the form {x∈ℝ≥0d:U⁡(x)≤M}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}_{\geq 0}:U(x)\leq M\} are compact for any finite constant MM. So (5.3) is proven.

Now, assume (5.4) does not hold: this implies that there exists 1≤i≤d1\leq i\leq d such that

infz⁡(0)∈Υinft≥0zi​(t)=0.\inf_{z(0)\in\Upsilon}\inf_{t\geq 0}z_{i}(t)=0.

For simplicity, in the rest of the proof we will denote by θ\theta an element of Υ\Upsilon and by zθ​(⋅)z_{\theta}(\cdot) the solution with zθ​(0)=θz_{\theta}(0)=\theta. Since

{zθ(t):θ∈Υ,t≥0}\{z_{\theta}(t)\,:\,\theta\in\Upsilon,t\geq 0\}

is contained in a compact set by (5.3), there must be an accumulation point ω∈∂ℝ≥0d\omega\in\partial\mathbb{R}^{d}_{\geq 0} with

infθ∈Υinft≥0‖zθ​(t)−ω‖∞=0.\inf_{\theta\in\Upsilon}\inf_{t\geq 0}\|z_{\theta}(t)-\omega\|_{\infty}=0. (5.5)

Let 𝒮~⊆𝒮\tilde{\mathcal{S}}\subseteq\mathcal{S} be the species whose entries are zero in ω\omega. Note that 𝒮~\tilde{\mathcal{S}} is not empty because ω∈∂ℝ≥0d\omega\in\partial\mathbb{R}^{d}_{\geq 0}, and for convenience denote by d~\tilde{d} its cardinality. Consider the associated reaction network 𝒢~\tilde{\mathcal{G}}, as described in Lemma 5.2, and consider the parameter dependent time variable rate functions

λ~y~→y~′​(x~,t,θ)=κ~y~→y~′​(t,θ)​x~y~for all ​x~∈ℝd~,θ∈Υ,y~→y~′∈ℛ~,\tilde{\lambda}_{\tilde{y}\to\tilde{y}^{\prime}}(\tilde{x},t,\theta)=\tilde{\kappa}_{\tilde{y}\to\tilde{y}^{\prime}}(t,\theta)\tilde{x}^{\tilde{y}}\quad\text{for all }\tilde{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{\tilde{d}},\theta\in\Upsilon,\tilde{y}\to\tilde{y}^{\prime}\in\tilde{\mathcal{R}},

where

κ~y~→y~′​(t,θ)=∑y→y′p⁡(y)=y~,p⁡(y′)=y~′κy→y′​zθ​(t)yp​(zθ​(t))y~.\tilde{\kappa}_{\tilde{y}\to\tilde{y}^{\prime}}(t,\theta)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}y\to y^{\prime}\\ p(y)=\tilde{y},p(y^{\prime})=\tilde{y}^{\prime}\end{subarray}}\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}\frac{z_{\theta}(t)^{y}}{p(z_{\theta}(t))^{\tilde{y}}}.

Note that we are essentially placing the influence of those species which are not equal to zero at ω\omega into the (now time-dependent) rate constants. It follows that

p⁡(zθ​(t))=p⁡(zθ​(0))+∑y~→y~′∈ℛ~(y~′−y~)​∫0tλ~y~→y~′​(p⁡(zθ​(s)),s,θ)​𝑑s.p(z_{\theta}(t))=p(z_{\theta}(0))+\sum_{\tilde{y}\to\tilde{y}^{\prime}\in\tilde{\mathcal{R}}}(\tilde{y}^{\prime}-\tilde{y})\int_{0}^{t}\tilde{\lambda}_{\tilde{y}\to\tilde{y}^{\prime}}(p(z_{\theta}(s)),s,\theta)\,ds.

Moreover, 𝒢~\tilde{\mathcal{G}} is strongly endotactic by Lemma 5.2. Note that in a neighborhood of ω\omega the functions κ~y~→y~′​(t,θ)\tilde{\kappa}_{\tilde{y}\to\tilde{y}^{\prime}}(t,\theta) satisfy (5.1) because the entries relative to species that are not in 𝒮~\tilde{\mathcal{S}} are bounded away from 0. Hence from (5.5) it follows that the solutions p​(zθ​(⋅))p(z_{\theta}(\cdot)) get arbitrarily close to the origin (of ℝd~\mathbb{R}^{\tilde{d}}), but this is in contradiction with the second part of Corollary 5.1 and the proof is concluded. ∎

We now state and prove here the main results of [24]. The proofs we propose rely on Corollary 5.1 and Lemma 5.3, and have substantial similarities with the techniques developed in [5, 4, 24].

Theorem 5.4.

Consider a deterministic mass action system (𝒢,Λ)(\mathcal{G},\Lambda), and assume 𝒢\mathcal{G} is strongly endotactic. Then, (𝒢,Λ)(\mathcal{G},\Lambda) is persistent.

Proof.

The theorem just follows from Lemma 5.3, in particular from (5.4), by considering Υ=z⁡(0)∈ℝ>0d\Upsilon=z(0)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0}. ∎

Theorem 5.5.

Consider a deterministic mass action system (𝒢,Λ)(\mathcal{G},\Lambda), and assume 𝒢\mathcal{G} is strongly endotactic. Then, (𝒢,Λ)(\mathcal{G},\Lambda) is permanent.

Proof.

Fix a set SyS_{y} as in Definition 5.2, and let Γ⊂Sy\Gamma\subset S_{y} be as in Corollary 5.1 (the result applies if we consider the rates κy→y′​(t,θ)\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t,\theta) to be constant functions). Since Γ⊂ℝ>0d\Gamma\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0}, there exists ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that the enlarged set

Υ={x∈Sy:infz∈Γ‖x−z‖∞≤ε}⊂ℝ>0d.\Upsilon=\{x\in S_{y}\,:\,\inf_{z\in\Gamma}\|x-z\|_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0}.

Moreover, note that Υ\Upsilon is a compact set and Γ⊂Υ\Gamma\subset\Upsilon. Our first goal is to prove that every trajectory {z⁡(t):t≥0}\{z(t)\,:\,t\geq 0\} with z⁡(0)∈Syz(0)\in S_{y} intersects Υ\Upsilon.

Let

τ=inf{t≥0:dd​t​U​(z⁡(t))>0}.\tau=\inf\left\{t\geq 0\,:\,\frac{d}{dt}U(z(t))>0\right\}.

If τ<∞\tau<\infty, then by Corollary 5.1, and since Γ\Gamma is compact, we have z⁡(τ)∈Γ⊂Υz(\tau)\in\Gamma\subset\Upsilon. Now suppose that τ=∞\tau=\infty. Since U⁡(⋅)U(\cdot) has a lower bound, the function UU can not decrease indefinitely along z⁡(⋅)z(\cdot). Thus, we must have

lim supt→∞dd​t​U​(z⁡(t))≥0.\limsup_{t\to\infty}\frac{d}{dt}U(z(t))\geq 0.

Hence, by Corollary 5.1 and by compactness of Γ\Gamma the closure of {z⁡(t):t≥0}\{z(t)\,:\,t\geq 0\} intersects Γ\Gamma, which implies that {z⁡(t):t≥0}\{z(t)\,:\,t\geq 0\} intersects Υ\Upsilon. In conclusion, we have proved that every trajectory starting in SyS_{y} intersects the compact set Υ\Upsilon at a certain finite time. Then, permanence follows from Lemma 5.3 by choosing

K={x∈Sy:min1≤i≤d⁡xi≥m​ and ​‖x‖∞≤M}K=\{x\in S_{y}\,:\,\min_{1\leq i\leq d}x_{i}\geq m\text{ and }\|x\|_{\infty}\leq M\}

where

m\displaystyle m =min1≤i≤dinfz⁡(0)∈Υinft≥0zi(t)>0\displaystyle=\min_{1\leq i\leq d}\inf_{z(0)\in\Upsilon}\inf_{t\geq 0}z_{i}(t)>0
M\displaystyle M =supz⁡(0)∈Υsupt≥0‖z⁡(t)‖∞<∞.\displaystyle=\sup_{z(0)\in\Upsilon}\sup_{t\geq 0}\|z(t)\|_{\infty}<\infty.

This concludes the proof. ∎

6 Asiphonic Strongly Endotactic Networks and Large Deviation Principle

In this section, we consider large deviations of classically scaled reaction networks. In particular, we focus on the results [2, 1], which are derived from a sufficient condition that will be denoted as Assumption 1 later in this paper. We utilize the findings of section 4 to prove this condition holds in a straightforward manner.

For convenience, throughout this section we denote f⁡(x)≈g⁡(x)f(x)\approx g(x) or we say f⁡(x)f(x) grows like g⁡(x)g(x), if

0<lim‖x‖1→∞f⁡(x)g⁡(x)<∞.0<\lim_{\|x\|_{1}\to\infty}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}<\infty.

Following [29, 30] we introduce the family of classically scaled process indexed by a real number V>0V>0. In particular, we assume the process associated with VV is a stochastic mass action system with rate constant κy→y′/V‖y‖1−1\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}/V^{\|y\|_{1}-1}, where κy→y′\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}} is a fixed positive constant. Hence, for a particular choice of V>0V>0, the intensity function for y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} is

λy→y′V(x)=κy→y′V‖y‖1−1𝟙{x≥y}x!(x−y)!, for x∈ℤ≥0d.\lambda_{y\to y^{\prime}}^{V}(x)=\frac{\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}}{V^{\|y\|_{1}-1}}\mathbbm{1}_{\{x\geq y\}}\frac{x!}{(x-y)!},\quad\text{ for }x\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}_{\geq 0}.

We then denote the resulting stochastic process detailed in section 2.4 by XVX^{V}. Next, we consider the scaled process

X¯V​(t)=V−1​XV​(t)∈V−1​ℤ≥0d.\overline{X}^{V}(t)=V^{-1}X^{V}(t)\in V^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^{d}_{\geq 0}. (6.1)

The associated transition intensities for the process X¯V\overline{X}^{V} are

λy→y′S,V​(x)=λy→y′V​(V​x)=κy→y′V‖y‖1−1​(V​x)!(V​x−y)!,x∈V−1​ℤ≥0d,\lambda^{S,V}_{y\to y^{\prime}}(x)=\lambda^{V}_{y\to y^{\prime}}(Vx)=\frac{\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}}{V^{\|y\|_{1}-1}}\frac{(Vx)!}{(Vx-y)!},\quad x\in V^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^{d}_{\geq 0}, (6.2)

and the generator is

(ℒV​f)​(x)=∑y→y′∈ℛλy→y′S,V​(x)​(f⁡(x+y′−yV)−f⁡(x)),x∈V−1​ℤ≥0d.(\mathcal{L}_{V}f)(x)=\sum_{y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\lambda^{S,V}_{y\to y^{\prime}}(x)\left(f\left(x+\frac{y^{\prime}-y}{V}\right)-f(x)\right),\quad x\in V^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^{d}_{\geq 0}. (6.3)

Following [2, 1], we are interested in finding conditions for a reaction network to satisfy a large deviation principle (LDP). By standard arguments, we see that for a fixed x∈ℝ>0dx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0} and VV large

λy→y′S,V​(⌊V​x⌋V)=κy→y′V‖y‖1−1​(⌊V​x⌋)!(⌊V​x⌋−y)!≈κy→y′V‖y‖1−1​V‖y‖1​xy=V​κy→y′​xy.\lambda_{y\to y^{\prime}}^{S,V}\left(\frac{\lfloor Vx\rfloor}{V}\right)=\frac{\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}}{V^{\|y\|_{1}-1}}\frac{(\lfloor Vx\rfloor)!}{(\lfloor Vx\rfloor-y)!}\approx\frac{\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}}{V^{\|y\|_{1}-1}}V^{\|y\|_{1}}x^{y}=V\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}x^{y}.

Hence, we also define the analogous “deterministic” intensity function

λy→y′D,V​(x)=V​κy→y′​xy, for ​x∈ℝ≥0d.\lambda_{y\to y^{\prime}}^{D,V}(x)=V\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}x^{y},\quad\text{ for }x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}_{\geq 0}. (6.4)

For completeness, we provide the definition for a LDP in the setting of reaction networks. Following the notations in [1] and [2], we denote by D0,T​(ℝ>0d)D_{0,T}(\mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0}) the Skorokhod space, or space of ca`\grave{a}dla`\grave{a}g functions z:[0,T]→ℝ≥0dz:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}^{d}_{\geq 0}, equipped with the topology of uniform convergence.

Definition 6.1.

Fix a positive T<∞T<\infty and a lower semi-continuous mapping I:D0,T​(ℝ>0d)→[0,∞]I:D_{0,T}(\mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0})\to[0,\infty] such that for any α∈ℝ>0\alpha\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}, the level set {z:I⁡(z)≤α}\{z:I(z)\leq\alpha\} is a compact subset of D0,T​(ℝ>0d)D_{0,T}(\mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0}). The probability distribution of sample paths of the processes {X¯V}V>0\big\{\overline{X}^{V}\big\}_{V>0} with fixed initial condition X¯V​(0)=x∈ℝ>0d\overline{X}^{V}(0)=x\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{d} obeys a LDP with good rate function I⁡(⋅)I(\cdot) if for any measurable Γ⊂D0,T​(ℝ>0d)\Gamma\subset D_{0,T}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{d}) we have

−infz∈ΓoI(z)\displaystyle-\inf_{z\in\Gamma^{o}}I(z) ≤lim infV→∞1V​ln⁡(P⁡(X¯V​(t)∈Γ|X¯V​(0)=x))\displaystyle\leq\liminf_{V\to\infty}\frac{1}{V}\ln\left(P\left(\overline{X}^{V}(t)\in\Gamma\ \big|\ \overline{X}^{V}(0)=x\right)\right)
≤lim supV→∞1Vln(P(X¯V(t)∈Γ|X¯V(0)=x))≤−infz∈Γ¯I(z)\displaystyle\leq\limsup_{V\to\infty}\frac{1}{V}\ln\left(P\left(\overline{X}^{V}(t)\in\Gamma\ \big|\ \overline{X}^{V}(0)=x\right)\right)\leq-\inf_{z\in\bar{\Gamma}}I(z)

where Γo\Gamma^{o} and Γ¯\bar{\Gamma} denote the interior and closure of Γ\Gamma respectively.

In [1], it is shown that under Assumption 1 below, the process X¯V\overline{X}^{V} satisfies a sample path LDP in the supremum norm.

Assumption 1.

Let X¯V\overline{X}^{V} be the process (6.1). We assume

  1. 1.

    There exists b<∞b<\infty and a continuous, positive function U⁡(⋅)U(\cdot) with compact sublevel sets, such that for some non-decreasing function v′:ℝ>0→ℝ>0v^{\prime}:\mathbb{R}_{>0}\to\mathbb{R}_{>0},

    (ℒV​UV)​(x)≤eb​V∀V>v′​(‖x‖1),x∈V−1​ℤ≥0d(\mathcal{L}_{V}U^{V})(x)\leq e^{bV}\qquad\forall V>v^{\prime}(\|x\|_{1}),\qquad x\in V^{-1}\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{d} (6.5)

    where UV​(⋅)U^{V}(\cdot) denotes the Vt​hV^{th} power of U⁡(⋅)U(\cdot), and ℒV\mathcal{L}_{V} is defined as in (6.3).

  2. 2.

    With positive probability, starting at X¯V​(0)=0\overline{X}^{V}(0)=0, the Markov process X¯V\overline{X}^{V} reaches in finite time some state x+x_{+} in the strictly positive orthant V−1​ℤ>0dV^{-1}\mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{d}.

Moreover, [1] and [2] show that Assumption 1 holds for reaction networks with a certain structure. We require the following definition before stating their result.

Definition 6.2.

A non-empty subset 𝒫⊂𝒮={S1,…,Sd}\mathcal{P}\subset\mathcal{S}=\{S_{1},\dots,S_{d}\} is called a siphon if for every reaction y→y′∈ℛy\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} the following condition holds: if yi′>0y^{\prime}_{i}>0 for some Si∈𝒫S_{i}\in\mathcal{P}, then yj>0y_{j}>0 for some Sj∈𝒫S_{j}\in\mathcal{P}. A reaction network is called asiphonic if no such 𝒫\mathcal{P} exists.

In words, 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a siphon if every reaction whose product complex contains an element of 𝒫\mathcal{P} also has an element of 𝒫\mathcal{P} in its source complex. Note that if a network is asiphonic, then 0∈𝒞S0\in\mathcal{C}^{S} (the set of source complexes) for otherwise 𝒮\mathcal{S} would be a siphon.

Theorem 6.1.

If the network is asiphonic and strongly endotactic (ASE), then the Markov process X¯V\overline{X}^{V} satisfies Assumption (1) with UU defined as in (4.6) (which is the usual Lyapunov function) and the function v′​(x)=exv^{\prime}(x)=e^{x}.

Note that there is a simple argument showing that asiphonic reaction networks automatically satisfy the second part of Assumption 1 (see Remark 1.11 in [1]). It is significantly harder to show ASE reaction networks satisfy the first condition in Assumption 1. Here we will provide a proof showing that ASE reaction networks satisfy the first condition of Assumption 1, and will do so using a tier structure argument. Specifically, we will prove Theorem 6.2 below, which implies Theorem 6.1, and is the main result of this section.

Theorem 6.2.

Suppose the reaction network (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) is ASE. Furthermore, let UU be defined as in (4.6) and let v′​(x)=exv^{\prime}(x)=e^{x}. Then there exists a compact set B⊂ℝdB\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} such that for all pairs (V,x)(V,x) satisfying V>v′​(‖x‖1)=e‖x‖1V>v^{\prime}(\|x\|_{1})=e^{\|x\|_{1}}, x∈V−1​ℤ≥0dx\in V^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^{d}_{\geq 0}, and x∈Bcx\in B^{c}, we have

(ℒV​UV)​(x)<0.(\mathcal{L}_{V}U^{V})(x)<0. (6.6)

Before getting to the proof of the Theorem, we need a preliminary technical result which we prove using the tier sequence technique. Later when we prove the theorem, it will be apparent that the term H⁡(xn,Vn)H(x_{n},V_{n}) in Lemma 6.3 determines the sign of (ℒV​UV)​(x)(\mathcal{L}_{V}U^{V})(x).

Lemma 6.3.

Suppose that there is a sequence (xn,Vn)n=0∞(x_{n},V_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} such that:

∙(xn)n=0∞ is a tier sequence\displaystyle\bullet\quad(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty}\quad\text{ is a tier sequence} (6.7)
∙limn→∞‖xn‖1=∞\displaystyle\bullet\quad\lim_{n\to\infty}\|x_{n}\|_{1}=\infty\hskip 216.81pt\phantom{.} (6.8)
∙Vn>e‖xn‖1 and xn∈Vn−1​ℤ>0d.\displaystyle\bullet\quad V_{n}>e^{\|x_{n}\|_{1}}\quad\text{ and }\quad x_{n}\in V_{n}^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^{d}_{>0}. (6.9)

Let c1∈ℝc_{1}\in\mathbb{R} and c2∈ℝ>0c_{2}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} and let

H⁡(xn,Vn)=∑y→y′∈ℛκy→y′​xny​U​(xn)​(exp⁡(ln⁡(xny′−y)+c1c2​U​(xn))−1).\displaystyle H(x_{n},V_{n})=\sum_{y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}x_{n}^{y}U(x_{n})\bigg(\exp\bigg(\frac{\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\prime}-y})+c_{1}}{c_{2}U(x_{n})}\bigg)-1\bigg). (6.10)

Then

lim infn→∞H⁡(xn,Vn)=−∞.\displaystyle\liminf_{n\to\infty}H(x_{n},V_{n})=-\infty. (6.11)
Proof.

Note that U⁡(xn)U(x_{n}) grows like ‖xn‖1​ln⁡(‖xn‖1)\|x_{n}\|_{1}\ln(\|x_{n}\|_{1}), as n→∞n\to\infty, which itself converges to ∞\infty by (6.8). Thus it must be that lim supn→∞ln⁡(xn,i)U⁡(xn)≤0\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\ln(x_{n,i})}{U(x_{n})}\leq 0 for each i∈{1,…,d}i\in\{1,\dots,d\}. Let us consider the set of indices

E={i:lim infn→∞ln⁡(xn,i)U⁡(xn)<0}.\displaystyle E=\left\{i:\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\ln(x_{n,i})}{U(x_{n})}<0\right\}.

The set EE can be non-empty, and consists of the indices of those species which are in relatively low abundance. To make this notion more concrete, we illustrate it with an example that is not part of the proof. Consider a two-dimensional system with xn=(e−n2,n)x_{n}=(e^{-n^{2}},n) and Vn=en2V_{n}=e^{n^{2}}. In this case, ln⁡(xn,1)=−n2\ln(x_{n,1})=-n^{2} whereas U⁡(xn)U(x_{n}) grows like n​ln⁡(n)n\ln(n) as n→∞n\to\infty. Thus, limn→∞ln⁡(xn,1)U⁡(xn)=−∞\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\ln(x_{n,1})}{U(x_{n})}=-\infty and 1∈E1\in E.

We now return to the proof. By potentially considering another subsequence, we may replace all the lim inf\liminf and lim sup\limsup by lim\lim in the above. Using EE, we can partition the set of reactions ℛ\mathcal{R} into 3 mutually exclusive groups: those that consume a species in EE, those that produce a species in EE but do not consume one, and those that neither consume nor produce a species in EE. Specifically, we let

  • •

    ℛ1={y→y′:yi≠0​for some​i∈E}\mathcal{R}_{1}=\{y\to y^{\prime}:y_{i}\neq 0\ \text{for some}\ i\in E\},

  • •

    ℛ2={y→y′:yi=0​∀i∈E​and​yi′≠0​for some​i∈E}\mathcal{R}_{2}=\{y\to y^{\prime}:y_{i}=0\ \forall i\in E\ \text{and}\ y^{\prime}_{i}\neq 0\ \text{for some}\ i\in E\}, and

  • •

    ℛ3={y→y′:yi=yi′=0​∀i∈E}\mathcal{R}_{3}=\{y\to y^{\prime}:y_{i}=y^{\prime}_{i}=0\ \forall i\in E\}.

Note that because the network is asiphonic, 0∈𝒞S0\in\mathcal{C}^{S}. Hence, ℛ1≠ℛ\mathcal{R}_{1}\neq\mathcal{R}. We then decompose HH in the obvious manner as H⁡(xn,Vn)=H1​(xn,Vn)+H2​(xn,Vn)+H3​(xn,Vn),H(x_{n},V_{n})=H_{1}(x_{n},V_{n})+H_{2}(x_{n},V_{n})+H_{3}(x_{n},V_{n}), where

Hi​(xn,Vn)=∑y→y′∈ℛiκy→y′​xny​U​(xn)​(exp⁡(ln⁡(xny′−y)+c1c2​U​(xn))−1).\displaystyle H_{i}(x_{n},V_{n})=\sum_{y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}_{i}}\kappa_{y\to y^{\prime}}x_{n}^{y}U(x_{n})\bigg(\exp\bigg(\frac{\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\prime}-y})+c_{1}}{c_{2}U(x_{n})}\bigg)-1\bigg).

We will prove that reactions from ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1} give insignificant contribution to the network dynamics along a tier sequence, while there are “good” reactions in ℛ2\mathcal{R}_{2} and ℛ3\mathcal{R}_{3} that help stabilizing the dynamics by consuming species with high abundance. Specifically, we will show that (i) limn→∞H1​(xn,Vn)=0\lim_{n\to\infty}H_{1}(x_{n},V_{n})=0, (ii) the terms in H2H_{2} are negative, and (iii) the negative terms in H2H_{2} and H3H_{3} are sufficient to guarantee that (6.11) holds.

We turn to H1​(xn,Vn)H_{1}(x_{n},V_{n}). First note that for y→y′∈ℛ1y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}_{1}, we have that

ln(xny′−y)=⟨y′,ln(xn)⟩−⟨y,ln(xn)⟩≤c3∑i∈E|ln(xn,i)|=−c3∑i∈Eln(xn,i),\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\prime}-y})=\langle y^{\prime},\ln(x_{n})\rangle-\langle y,\ln(x_{n})\rangle\leq c_{3}\sum_{i\in E}|\ln(x_{n,i})|=-c_{3}\sum_{i\in E}\ln(x_{n,i}),

for some positive constant c3c_{3}. Hence, there is a c4>0c_{4}>0 so that for nn large enough

xny​U​(xn)​exp⁡(CLOSEOPENln⁡(xny′−y)+c1c2​U​(xn))≤xny​U​(xn)​exp⁡(−c4​∑i∈Eln⁡(xn,i)U⁡(xn))=exp⁡(∑i=1dyi​ln⁡(xn,i)+ln⁡(U⁡(xn))−∑i∈Ec4​ln⁡(xn,i)U⁡(xn))=exp⁡(∑i∈Eln⁡(xn,i)​(yi−c4U⁡(xn))+∑j∉Eyj​ln⁡(xn,j)+ln⁡(U⁡(xn))).\displaystyle\begin{split}x_{n}^{y}U(x_{n})\exp\bigg(&\frac{\ln(x_{n}^{y^{\prime}-y})+c_{1}}{c_{2}U(x_{n})}\bigg)\leq x_{n}^{y}U(x_{n})\exp\bigg(-\frac{c_{4}\sum_{i\in E}\ln(x_{n,i})}{U(x_{n})}\bigg)\\ &=\exp\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{d}y_{i}\ln(x_{n,i})+\ln(U(x_{n}))-\frac{\sum_{i\in E}c_{4}\ln(x_{n,i})}{U(x_{n})}\bigg)\\ &=\exp\bigg(\sum_{i\in E}\ln(x_{n,i})\bigg(y_{i}-\frac{c_{4}}{U(x_{n})}\bigg)+\sum_{j\notin E}y_{j}\ln(x_{n,j})+\ln(U(x_{n}))\bigg).\end{split} (6.12)

Note that from the construction of EE, for i∈Ei\in E and j∉Ej\notin E, we must have |ln⁡(xn,i)|≫ln⁡(U⁡(xn))|\ln(x_{n,i})|\gg\ln(U(x_{n})) and |ln⁡(xn,i)|≫ln⁡(xn,j)|\ln(x_{n,i})|\gg\ln(x_{n,j}). Since yi≥1y_{i}\geq 1 for some i∈Ei\in E, we must have

7 Network conditions for positive recurrence of strongly endotactic reaction networks

As we showed in Example 3.1 and Example 3.2, strong endotacticity is not a sufficient condition for positive recurrence of the associated Markov model introduced in section 2.4. Thus, in this section we provide additional network conditions for strongly endotactic reaction networks that guarantee positive recurrence. We note that while the previous section considered families of models under the “classical scaling,” this section does not. We therefore drop the VV-dependence in the notation. For example, the generator will now be denoted as ℒ\mathcal{L} instead of ℒV\mathcal{L}_{V}.

We require two definitions.

Definition 7.1.

A reaction network (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) is binary if ‖y‖1≤2\|y\|_{1}\leq 2 for each y∈𝒞y\in\mathcal{C}.

Many reaction networks in biology and chemistry are binary as it is rare that more than two molecules would interact simultaneously.

Definition 7.2.

The reactions 0→S0\rightarrow S and S→0S\rightarrow 0 are the in-flow and out-flow of species S∈𝒮S\in\mathcal{S}, respectively. A reaction network is fully open if 0→S∈ℛ0\to S\in\mathcal{R} and S→0∈ℛS\to 0\in\mathcal{R} for each S∈𝒮S\in\mathcal{S}.

The main theorem provided in this section, Theorem 7.2 below, will allow us to conclude that, for example, the Markov process associated with a reaction network that is a union of (i) a binary, strongly endotactic network, and (ii) some in-flows and all out-flows, is necessarily positive recurrent. This is made precise in the following corollary.

Corollary 7.1.

Let (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) be a binary, strongly endotactic reaction network. Let ℛout\mathcal{R}_{\text{out}} be the union of outflows, ∪S{S→0}\cup_{S}\{S\to 0\}, and let ℛin\mathcal{R}_{\text{in}} be a subset of the inflows, ∪S{0→S}\cup_{S}\{0\to S\}. Then let

ℛ~=ℛ∪ℛout∪ℛin\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}=\mathcal{R}\cup\mathcal{R}_{\text{out}}\cup\mathcal{R}_{\text{in}}

and 𝒞~=𝒞∪{S∈𝒮}∪{0}.\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}=\mathcal{C}\cup\{S\in\mathcal{S}\}\cup\{0\}. Then, for any choice of rate constants, the Markov process with reaction network (𝒮,𝒞~,ℛ~)(\mathcal{S},\widetilde{\mathcal{C}},\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}) and stochastic mass action kinetics satisfies the following: each state in a closed, irreducible component of the state space is positive recurrent; moreover, if τx0\tau_{x_{0}} is the time for the process to enter the union of the closed irreducible components given an initial condition x0x_{0}, then 𝔼⁡[τx0]<∞\mathbb{E}[\tau_{x_{0}}]<\infty.

Note that Corollary 7.1 implies that if a reaction network, (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) is strongly endotactic, binary, and fully open, then the associated Markov model is necessarily positive recurrent, regardless of the choice of rate constants. This follows since in this case, (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)=(𝒮,𝒞~,ℛ~)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R})=(\mathcal{S},\widetilde{\mathcal{C}},\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}).

We also note that when (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)≠(𝒮,𝒞~,ℛ~)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R})\neq(\mathcal{S},\widetilde{\mathcal{C}},\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}) in Corollary 7.1, the resulting reaction network (𝒮,𝒞~,ℛ~)(\mathcal{S},\widetilde{\mathcal{C}},\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}) may not be strongly endotactic. We provide an example.

Example 7.1.

Consider the reaction network with species 𝒮={S1,S2}\mathcal{S}=\{S_{1},S_{2}\} and reactions

2​S1⇄S1+S2.2S_{1}\rightleftarrows S_{1}+S_{2}.

This network is binary and strongly endotactic (for example, this follows because the network is weakly reversible and consists of a single linkage class [24]). However, the fully open network

2​S1⇄S1+S2S1⇄0⇄S2,\displaystyle\begin{split}2S_{1}&\rightleftarrows S_{1}+S_{2}\\ S_{1}&\rightleftarrows 0\rightleftarrows S_{2},\end{split} (7.1)

is not strongly endotactic. This can be seen by noting that the transversal tier sequence (n,n)(n,n) is not tier descending. Of course, by Corollary 7.1 the fully open network (7.1) is positive recurrent for any choice of rate constants. □\square

Corollary 7.1 is a special case of Theorem 7.2 below, which can be seen as a generalization to non-binary reaction networks. In Theorem 7.2, the role of ℛout\mathcal{R}_{\text{out}} and ℛin\mathcal{R}_{\text{in}} is played by the sets of reactions ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} and ℛ′′\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}, respectively, which are defined below. Specifically, ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} is a set of reactions that decrease the total number of molecules, and ℛ′′\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime} is a set of reactions that increase it. The reactions in ℛ′′\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime} are not used in the proof, and are considered in Theorem 7.2 only to add to the generality of the result. The reactions in ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime}, on the other hand, play an important role in the proof of positive recurrence, and as illustrated in Example 3.1 the statement would not hold true without the inclusion of ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime}.

Let (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) be a reaction network with 𝒮={S1,…,Sd}\mathcal{S}=\{S_{1},\dots,S_{d}\} and m=max⁡{‖y‖1:y∈𝒞S}m=\max\{\|y\|_{1}:y\in\mathcal{C}^{S}\}. We remind the reader that 𝒞S\mathcal{C}^{S} denotes the set of source complexes. Next, for Si∈𝒮S_{i}\in\mathcal{S}, we let ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i} be a nonempty, finite subset of

{a​Si→∑j=1drj′​Sj:a≥m−1​ and ​∑j=1drj′≤a−1}\left\{aS_{i}\to\sum_{j=1}^{d}r_{j}^{\prime}S_{j}:a\geq m-1\text{ and }\sum_{j=1}^{d}r_{j}^{\prime}\leq a-1\right\}

and let

ℛ′=∪i=1dℛi.\mathcal{R}^{\prime}=\cup_{i=1}^{d}\mathcal{R}_{i}.

Let 𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime} be the set of complexes associated with the reactions in ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime}. Next, we let ℛ′′\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime} be a subset of

{∑j=1drj​Sj→∑j=1drj′​Sj:∑j=1drj≤m−2}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{d}r_{j}S_{j}\to\sum_{j=1}^{d}r_{j}^{\prime}S_{j}:\sum_{j=1}^{d}r_{j}\leq m-2\right\}

and let 𝒞′′\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime} be the set of complexes associated with the reactions in ℛ′′\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}. Note that it is possible, though not required, that either ℛ′⊂ℛ\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{R} or ℛ′′⊂ℛ\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}\subset\mathcal{R}. It is also possible that ℛ′′=∅\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}=\emptyset.

Theorem 7.2.

Let (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) be a strongly endotactic reaction network with 𝒮={S1,S2,…,Sd}\mathcal{S}=\{S_{1},S_{2},\dots,S_{d}\} and let m=max⁡{‖y‖1:y∈𝒞S}m=\max\{\|y\|_{1}:y\in\mathcal{C}^{S}\}. Let ℛ′,ℛ′′,𝒞′,\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime},\mathcal{C}^{\prime}, and 𝒞′′\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime} be as above and let ℛ~=ℛ∪ℛ′∪ℛ′′\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}=\mathcal{R}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime} and 𝒞~=𝒞∪𝒞′∪𝒞′′\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}=\mathcal{C}\cup\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\cup\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}. We assume further that

maxy→y′∈ℛ′⁡‖y′‖1<miny→y′∈ℛ′⁡‖y‖1.\max_{y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}^{\prime}}\|y^{\prime}\|_{1}<\min_{y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}^{\prime}}\|y\|_{1}. (7.2)

Then, for any choice of rate constants, the Markov process with reaction network (𝒮,𝒞~,ℛ~)(\mathcal{S},\widetilde{\mathcal{C}},\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}) and stochastic mass action kinetics satisfies the following: each state in a closed, irreducible component of the state space is positive recurrent; moreover, if τx0\tau_{x_{0}} is the time for the process to enter the union of the closed irreducible components given an initial condition x0x_{0}, then 𝔼⁡[τx0]<∞\mathbb{E}[\tau_{x_{0}}]<\infty.

Corollary 7.1 follows from Theorem 7.2 by considering the case m=2m=2.

To prove Theorem 7.2, we require the following well-known result, sometimes referred to as the “Foster-Lyapunov criterion.” For completeness, we include here a proof that makes use of the techniques developed in [32], which we refer to for more on this topic.

Theorem 7.3.

Let XX be a continuous-time Markov process on a state space 𝕊⊆ℤ≥0d\mathbb{S}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{d} with generator ℒ\mathcal{L}. Suppose there exists a finite set K⊂𝕊K\subset\mathbb{S} and a function U:𝕊→ℝ≥0U\colon\mathbb{S}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} such that U⁡(x)U(x) tends to infinity as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty and

(ℒ​U)​(x)≤−1\displaystyle(\mathcal{L}U)(x)\leq-1 (7.3)

for all x∈𝕊∖Kx\in\mathbb{S}\setminus K. Then each state in a closed, irreducible component of 𝕊\mathbb{S} is positive recurrent. Moreover, if τx0\tau_{x_{0}} is the time for the process to enter the union of the closed irreducible components given an initial condition x0x_{0}, then 𝔼⁡[τx0]<∞\mathbb{E}[\tau_{x_{0}}]<\infty.

Proof.

Non-explosivity follows from [32, Theorem 2.1], hence the random variable U⁡(X⁡(t))U(X(t)) is well-defined for all t>0t>0 and

sup0≤s≤tU⁡(X⁡(s))<∞a.s.\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}U(X(s))<\infty\quad\text{a.s.} (7.4)

for any t>0t>0 and any initial condition X⁡(0)=x0X(0)=x_{0}.

To conclude the proof, by standard arguments on continuous-time Markov chains [33], it is sufficient to show that the hitting time τK\tau_{K} of the finite set KK has finite expectation for any initial condition. For any M∈ℝ>0M\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}, let

τM=inf{t>0:U⁡(X⁡(t))≥M}.\tau_{M}=\inf\{t>0\,:\,U(X(t))\geq M\}.

By Dynkin’s formula, for any initial condition x0x_{0} and any M,t∈ℝ>0M,t\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}

E⁡[U⁡(X⁡(t∧τK∧τM))]\displaystyle E\left[U(X(t\wedge\tau_{K}\wedge\tau_{M}))\right] =U⁡(x0)+E⁡[∫0t∧τK∧τMℒ​U​(X⁡(s))​𝑑s]\displaystyle=U(x_{0})+E\left[\int_{0}^{t\wedge\tau_{K}\wedge\tau_{M}}\mathcal{L}U(X(s))ds\right]
≤U⁡(x0)−E⁡[t∧τK∧τM],\displaystyle\leq U(x_{0})-E\left[t\wedge\tau_{K}\wedge\tau_{M}\right],

and by non-negativity of UU we have

E⁡[t∧τK∧τM]≤U⁡(x0)<∞.E\left[t\wedge\tau_{K}\wedge\tau_{M}\right]\leq U(x_{0})<\infty. (7.5)

By (7.4), for any fixed t>0t>0 the random variable t∧τK∧τMt\wedge\tau_{K}\wedge\tau_{M} converges almost surely to t∧τKt\wedge\tau_{K}, as M→∞M\to\infty. Therefore, by the monotone convergence theorem and (7.5) we have

E⁡[t∧τK]≤U⁡(x0)<∞for all ​t∈ℝ>0.E\left[t\wedge\tau_{K}\right]\leq U(x_{0})<\infty\quad\text{for all }t\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}.

Since U⁡(x0)U(x_{0}) does not depend on tt, the stopping time τK\tau_{K} is almost surely finite. Hence, t∧τKt\wedge\tau_{K} converges almost surely to τK\tau_{K} as t→∞t\to\infty and by applying the monotone converge theorem again we obtain that E⁡[τK]E[\tau_{K}] is finite. ∎

The next lemma, introduced in [10, Lemma 4.1], provides an upper bound on (ℒ​U)​(xn)(\mathcal{L}U)(x_{n}), where (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} is a sequence in ℤ≥0d\mathbb{Z}^{d}_{\geq 0} satisfying limn→∞‖xn‖1=∞\lim_{n\to\infty}\|x_{n}\|_{1}=\infty, and UU is the usual Lyapunov function defined in (4.6).

Lemma 7.4.

Let ℒ\mathcal{L} be the generator of the Markov process associated with a reaction network (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) with stochastic mass-action kinetics (2.3). Let UU be the function defined in (4.6). For a sequence (xn)n=0∞(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty} in ℤ≥0d\mathbb{Z}^{d}_{\geq 0} such that limn→∞‖xn‖1=∞\lim_{n\to\infty}\|x_{n}\|_{1}=\infty, there is a constant C>0C>0 for which

(ℒ​U)​(xn)≤∑y→y′∈ℛλy→y′S​(xn)​(ln⁡((xn∨1)y′−y)+C),for every ​n≥0.\displaystyle(\mathcal{L}U)(x_{n})\leq\sum_{y\rightarrow y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}}\lambda^{S}_{y\to y^{\prime}}(x_{n})\left(\ln((x_{n}\vee 1)^{y^{\prime}-y})+C\right),\quad\text{for every }n\geq 0.

We will also require the following lemma in the proof of Theorem 7.2.

Lemma 7.5.

Let SS be the stoichiometric subspace of a reaction network (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}). Let (xn)n=0∞⊂ℤ≥0d(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty}\subset\mathbb{Z}^{d}_{\geq 0} be a sequence such that xn−xm∈Sx_{n}-x_{m}\in S for all n,m∈ℤ≥0n,m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. If (xn∨1)n=0∞(x_{n}\vee 1)_{n=0}^{\infty} is a tier sequence, then (xn∨1)n=0∞(x_{n}\vee 1)_{n=0}^{\infty} is transversal.

Proof.

The proof is essentially the same as that of Lemma 4.1, except xnx_{n} is replaced with xn∨1x_{n}\vee 1. ∎

Now we provide the proof of Theorem 7.2.

Proof (of Theorem 7.2).

Let 𝕊\mathbb{S} and SS be the state space of the associated Markov process XX and stochiometric subspace of (𝒮,𝒞~,ℛ~)(\mathcal{S},\widetilde{\mathcal{C}},\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}), respectively. We will show by contradiction that (7.3) holds with UU defined in (4.6).

Thus, we suppose that there exists a sequence (xn)n=0∞⊂𝕊(x_{n})_{n=0}^{\infty}\subset\mathbb{S} such that

limn→∞‖xn‖1=∞and(ℒ​U)​(xn)≥−1​ for all ​n.\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\|x_{n}\|_{1}=\infty\quad\text{and}\quad(\mathcal{L}U)(x_{n})\geq-1\text{ for all }n.

By Lemmma 7.4, there is a positive constant CC such that

(ℒ​U)​(xn)≤∑y→y′∈ℛ~λy→y′S​(xn)​(ln⁡((xn∨1)y′−y)+C).\displaystyle(\mathcal{L}U)(x_{n})\leq\sum_{y\rightarrow y^{\prime}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}}\lambda^{S}_{y\to y^{\prime}}(x_{n})\left(\ln{((x_{n}\vee 1)^{y^{\prime}-y})}+C\right). (7.6)

We will show that there exists a subsequence (xnk)k=0∞(x_{n_{k}})_{k=0}^{\infty} such that

limk→∞∑y→y′∈ℛ~λy→y′S​(xnk)​(ln⁡((xnk∨1)y′−y)+C)=−∞,\displaystyle\lim_{k\to\infty}\sum_{y\rightarrow y^{\prime}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}}\lambda^{S}_{y\to y^{\prime}}(x_{n_{k}})\left(\ln{((x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)^{y^{\prime}-y})}+C\right)=-\infty, (7.7)

in which case the proof is completed by contradiction.

By Remark 4.1, there must exist a subsequence (xnk∨1)k=0∞(x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)_{k=0}^{\infty} of (xn∨1)n=0∞(x_{n}\vee 1)_{n=0}^{\infty} which is a tier sequence. By Lemma 7.5, (xnk∨1)k=0∞(x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)_{k=0}^{\infty} is a transversal tier sequence. Since any subsequence of a transversal tier sequence is a transversal tier sequence, we can also assume that

  1. 1.

    for each reaction y→y′∈ℛ~y\to y^{\prime}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}, either λy→y′S​(xnk)≠0\lambda_{y\to y^{\prime}}^{S}(x_{n_{k}})\neq 0 for all kk or λy→y′S​(xnk)=0\lambda_{y\to y^{\prime}}^{S}(x_{n_{k}})=0 for all kk,

  2. 2.

    for each reaction y→y′∈ℛ~y\to y^{\prime}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}, we have limk→∞λy→y′S​ln⁡((xnk∨1)y′−y)∈[−∞,∞]\lim_{k\to\infty}\lambda^{S}_{y\to y^{\prime}}\ln{((x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)^{y^{\prime}-y})}\in[-\infty,\infty] and

  3. 3.

    there exists an index p∈{1,…,d}p\in\{1,\dots,d\} such that xnk,p≥xnk,ix_{n_{k},p}\geq x_{n_{k},i} for all k≥0k\geq 0 and all i∈{1,…,d}i\in\{1,\dots,d\}.

We note that since (xnk∨1)k=0∞(x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)_{k=0}^{\infty} is a tier sequence, xnk,p→∞x_{n_{k},p}\to\infty, as k→∞k\to\infty. We denote by a​Sp→ySpaS_{p}\to y_{S_{p}} a reaction from ℛp\mathcal{R}_{p}. Note that, by construction, ySp≺(xnk∨1)aSpy_{S_{p}}\prec_{(x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)}aS_{p} and that λa​Sp→ySpS​(xnk)→∞\lambda^{S}_{aS_{p}\to y_{S_{p}}}(x_{n_{k}})\to\infty, as k→∞k\to\infty.

We decompose ℛ~\widetilde{\mathcal{R}} into two parts,

ℛ~≾(xnk∨1)={y→y′∈ℛ~:y≾(xnk∨1)y′}and\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\precsim_{(x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)}}=\{y\to y^{\prime}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}:y\precsim_{(x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)}y^{\prime}\}\quad\text{and}
ℛ~≻(xnk∨1)={y→y′∈ℛ~:y≻(xnk∨1)y′}.\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\succ_{(x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)}}=\{y\to y^{\prime}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}:y\succ_{(x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)}y^{\prime}\}.

By (7.6) we have

(ℒ​U)​(xnk)≤\displaystyle(\mathcal{L}U)(x_{n_{k}})\leq ∑y→y′∈ℛ~≾(xnk∨1)λy→y′S(xnk)(ln((xnk∨1)y′−y)+C)\displaystyle\sum_{y\rightarrow y^{\prime}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\precsim_{(x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)}}}\lambda^{S}_{y\to y^{\prime}}(x_{n_{k}})\left(\ln{((x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)^{y^{\prime}-y})}+C\right) (7.8)
+∑y→y′∈ℛ~≻(xnk∨1)λy→y′S(xnk)(ln((xnk∨1)y′−y)+C).\displaystyle+\sum_{y\rightarrow y^{\prime}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\succ_{(x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)}}}\lambda^{S}_{y\to y^{\prime}}(x_{n_{k}})\left(\ln{((x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)^{y^{\prime}-y})}+C\right). (7.9)

For y→y′∈ℛ~≻(xnk∨1)y\to y^{\prime}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\succ_{(x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)}} we have

limk→∞λy→y′S​(xnk)​(ln⁡((xnk∨1)y′−y)+C)=−∞,\lim_{k\to\infty}\lambda^{S}_{y\to y^{\prime}}(x_{n_{k}})\left(\ln{((x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)^{y^{\prime}-y})}+C\right)=-\infty,

so long as λy→y′S​(xnk)≠0\lambda^{S}_{y\to y^{\prime}}(x_{n_{k}})\neq 0 for each kk. Moreover, aSp→ySp∈ℛ~≻(xnk∨1)aS_{p}\to y_{S_{p}}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\succ_{(x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)}} and λa​Sp→ySpS​(xnk)→∞\lambda^{S}_{aS_{p}\to y_{S_{p}}}(x_{n_{k}})\to\infty. Hence, the sum in (7.9) converges to −∞-\infty, as k→∞k\to\infty.

Turning to (7.8), we will show that for each y→y′∈ℛ~≾(xnk∨1)y\to y^{\prime}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\precsim_{(x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)}} there exists a y~→y~′∈ℛ~≻(xnk∨1)\tilde{y}\to\tilde{y}^{\prime}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\succ_{(x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)}} such that for any positive constant DD,

limk→∞(λy→y′S​(xnk)​(ln⁡((xnk∨1)y′−y)+C)+D​λy~→y~′S​(xnk)​(ln⁡((xnk∨1)y~′−y~)+C))=−∞,\displaystyle\lim_{k\to\infty}\left(\lambda^{S}_{y\to y^{\prime}}(x_{n_{k}})\left(\ln{((x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)^{y^{\prime}-y})}+C\right)+D\lambda^{S}_{\tilde{y}\to\tilde{y}^{\prime}}(x_{n_{k}})\left(\ln{((x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)^{\tilde{y}^{\prime}-\tilde{y}})}+C\right)\right)=-\infty, (7.10)

where CC is as in (7.6), which will complete the proof.

We now fix a reaction y→y′∈ℛ~≾(xnk∨1)y\to y^{\prime}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\precsim_{(x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)}}. We have three cases, depending upon the type of reaction:

Case 1. We assume y→y′∈ℛ∩ℛ~≾(xnk∨1)y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}\cap\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\precsim_{(x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)}}. for any choice of constants c1,c2∈ℝ>0c_{1},c_{2}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} and c3,c4∈ℝc_{3},c_{4}\in\mathbb{R}.

Note that if λy⋆→y⋆⁣⋆S​(xnk)≠0\lambda^{S}_{y^{\star}\to y^{\star\star}}(x_{n_{k}})\neq 0, then (6.23), with Vn=1V_{n}=1, and (7.11) together imply (7.10). Hence, we may assume that λy⋆→y⋆⁣⋆S​(xnk)=0\lambda^{S}_{y^{\star}\to y^{\star\star}}(x_{n_{k}})=0 for all kk. where we utilized (7.12) in the final inequality. Combining (7.14) and (7.15) shows

Case 2. We assume y→y′∈ℛ′∩ℛ~≾(xnk∨1)y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\cap\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\precsim_{(x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)}}. We may now combine (7.17) and (7.18) to conclude that (7.10) holds if we take y~→y~′=a​Sp→ySp\tilde{y}\to\tilde{y}^{\prime}=aS_{p}\to y_{S_{p}}. Specifically, for any D>0D>0,

Case 3. We assume y→y′∈ℛ′′∩ℛ~≾(xnk∨1)y\to y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}\cap\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\precsim_{(x_{n_{k}}\vee 1)}}. We will again show that (7.10) holds if we take y~→y~′=a​Sp→ySp\tilde{y}\to\tilde{y}^{\prime}=aS_{p}\to y_{S_{p}}.

Example 7.2.

Now we consider the strongly endotactic reaction network (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) introduced in Example 3.1.

0→2​A+B→4​A+4​B→A,\displaystyle 0\to 2A+B\to 4A+4B\to A, (7.20)

As we showed in Example 3.1, the associated Markov process for this reaction network is transient. Note that m=max⁡{‖y‖1:y∈𝒞S}=8m=\max\{\|y\|_{1}:y\in\mathcal{C}^{S}\}=8 for this reaction network. We let

ℛA={7A→5A+B},ℛB={7B→6B},ℛ′=ℛA∪ℛB,\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{A}=\{7A\to 5A+B\},\quad\mathcal{R}_{B}=\{7B\to 6B\},\quad\mathcal{R}^{\prime}=\mathcal{R}_{A}\cup\mathcal{R}_{B}, (7.21)

and 𝒞′={7​A,5​A+B,7​B,6​B}\mathcal{C}^{\prime}=\{7A,5A+B,7B,6B\}. Then by Theorem 7.2, the Markov process associated to (𝒮,C~,R~)(\mathcal{S},\widetilde{C},\widetilde{R}), where C~=𝒞∪𝒞′\widetilde{C}=\mathcal{C}\cup\mathcal{C}^{\prime} and R~=ℛ∪ℛ′\widetilde{R}=\mathcal{R}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\prime}, is positive recurrent for any choice of rate constants.

Note that we could even add extra reactions, via ℛ′′\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}, that seem to push the process away from the origin, and still reach the same conclusion. For example, we could let

ℛ′′={6A→10A+10B, 5A+B→110A+20B, 3A+2B→30B},\displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime}=\{6A\to 10A+10B,\ 5A+B\to 110A+20B,\ 3A+2B\to 30B\}, (7.22)

and

𝒞′′={6​A, 10​A+10​B, 5​A+B, 110​A+20​B, 3​A+2​B, 30​B}.\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}=\{6A,\ 10A+10B,\ 5A+B,\ 110A+20B,\ 3A+2B,\ 30B\}.

Then by Theorem 7.2, the Markov process associated to (𝒮,C~,R~)(\mathcal{S},\widetilde{C},\widetilde{R}), where

C~=𝒞∪𝒞′∪𝒞′′andR~=ℛ∪ℛ′∪ℛ′′,\widetilde{C}=\mathcal{C}\cup\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\cup\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}\quad\text{and}\quad\widetilde{R}=\mathcal{R}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\prime\prime},

is positive recurrent for all choice of rate constants. □\square
